A 45-year-old man presents with progressive weakness of his hands over nine months.
On examination he has fasciculations and wasting of the muscles of his upper limbs. Reﬂexes are brisk in his lower limbs and planters areupgoing. Sensation is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis in this gentleman?
explanation:
There is a mixture of lower motor neurone signs in the upper arms and upper motor neurone signs in the legs. This patient hasmotor neurone disease of the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis type.
Chronic inﬂammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) is an acquired immune mediated inﬂammatory disorder of theperipheral nervous system and is closely related to Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Patients usually present with a history of weakness, numbness and diﬃculty walking.
Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is an inﬂammatory disease resulting in slowly progressive weakness and wasting of both distal andproximal muscles.
Polymyositis is an inﬂammatory myopathy. Muscles may be painful and CK is markedly elevated.
Progressive muscular atrophy is a rare form of motor neurone disease which  affects only the lower motor neurones resulting infasciculations and progressive wasting of upper and lower limbs.

A 29-year-old man presents with a six month history of nasal congestion. He was seen by an ENT consultant who diagnosed sinusitis. Hepresents now with a two day history of right periorbital swelling and diplopia.
Examination reveals him to be unwell, although he has no neck stiffness or photophobia; his temperature is 37.4°C. He has marked droopingof the right eyelid with the right eye congested and deviated to the right with an enlarged right pupil. Left eye appears normal. Fundoscopy isnormal. There is also loss of sensation of the right forehead.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The history is typical for cavernous sinus thrombosis possibly secondary to sinusitis. This is a life threatening condition.
Urgent CT brain and antibiotics are needed.
The structures within and beside the cavernous sinus and their relative position can be memorised with the following mnemonic:
O TOM CAT
O TOM are the ﬁrst letters of structures of the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus arranged vertically, from the top to the bottom. CAare the ﬁrst letters of the structures located within the sinus. 
O: Oculomotor nerve
T: Trochlear nerve
O: Ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve
M: Maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve
C: Internal carotid artery
A: Abducent nerve

A 70-year-old man is referred with a six month history of increasing unsteadiness.
He describes an irregular swaying gait with a tendency to drift to the right when walking. His wife comments that he tends to keep his feetapart when standing. In addition he has noticed problems with urinary urgency and frequency. Multiple urine samples sent by his GP havefailed to detect infection. His muscles sometimes feel stiff but he puts this down to old age.
On examination, pulse is 72 beats/min, BP 140/85 mmHg lying, 110/60 mmHg standing.The muscles of the upper and lower limbs showincrease tone in the opposing muscle groups when the joints are passively moved. There is no obvious loss of muscle bulk. Power appears tobe normal in all muscle groups. Gait is broad-based with a tendency to lean to the right. Reﬂexes were brisk throughout and plantarresponses were downgoing bilaterally. Finger to nose testing is impaired in the upper limbs. Sensory examination is unremarkable.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple system atrophy is a degenerative disorder characterised by parkinsonian features, autonomic insuﬃciency (leading topostural hypotension, anhidrosis, disturbance of sphincter control, impotence) and signs of a cerebellar deﬁcit.
Chronic inﬂammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is clinically similar to Guillain-Barre syndrome (hyporeﬂexia or areﬂexia,paraesthesia and mild sensory deﬁcits in the upper and lower extremities, weakness) except that it follows a chronic progressivecourse.
Friedreich's ataxia is characterised by progressive gait ataxia, depressed knee and ankle reﬂexes, cerebellar signs, and impairment ofjoint position and vibration sense - clinical manifestations almost always begin to appear before puberty.
Polymyositis often presents with muscle weakness and wasting, especially of the proximal and girdle muscles, muscle pain andtenderness, weight loss and a low grade fever.

This 53-year-old man with diabetes who presents with headache and double vision was asked to look to his right.
What is the diagnosis?
options: Left third and sixth nerve palsies
Left third and seventh nerve palsies
explanation:
The third (oculomotor) nerve nucleus complex lies in the midbrain.
Motor neurones project to the ipsilateral medial rectus, inferior rectus, and internal oblique muscles and to the contralateral superiorrectus.
One central nucleus innervates levator palpebrae superioris bilaterally. Therefore a midbrain infarct that destroys the central nucleuswill result in bilateral ptosis.
Damage to the oculomotor nerve during its course results in ipsilateral ptosis; at rest, the globe is diverted downwards and laterally.The eye cannot be moved medially, superiorly or inferiorly. The effect on the pupil is variable, depending on the location of thelesion.

A 23-year-old intravenous drug user presents with bilateral groin abscesses.
After drainage of the abscesses he is started on intravenous ﬂucloxacillin and gentamicin. Twelve hours later he complained of diplopiawhich deteriorated, and also developed dysphagia and muscle weakness and needed ventilatory support.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Aminoglycosides may impair neuromuscular transmission and should not be given to patients with myasthenia gravis; large dosesgiven during surgery have been responsible for a transient myaesthenic syndrome in patients with normal neuromuscular function.
Non-depolarising muscle relaxants (also known as competitive muscle relaxants) compete with acetylcholine for receptor sites atthe neuromuscular junction. Non-depolarising muscle relaxants may be divided into theAminosteroid group (for example, pancuronium, vecuronium), and theBenzylisoquinolinium group (for example, atracurium).
Wound botulism is the other possible cause but the incubation period for wound botulism is longer, four to 14 days. It would presentin a similar way to this case with descending, afebrile, symmetric paralysis particularly affecting the cranial nerves. There is also anabsence of gastrointestinal symptoms which are common in botulism.

A 59-year-old right handed woman was referred to neurology clinic having developed tingling affecting her right hand. The tingling appearedworse at night and she had disrupted sleep as a result often needing to shake her hand to get rid of the tingling. She had also noticed recentproblems with grip particularly when manipulating ﬁne objects or unscrewing jam jar lids and was also beginning to experience an achingsensation radiating up the forearm. Sometimes she commented that her ﬁngers felt swollen.
She had a past medical history of hypothyroidism and diabetes, and took regular thyroxine and metformin. She worked in a supermarket onthe checkout tills and had noticed the problem since commencing work. She was a smoker of 10 cigarettes per day and drank 10 units ofalcohol per week.
On examination there was some mild wasting of the right thenar eminence with some fasciculations. Tone was normal in the ﬁngers. Onexamination of power there was reduced power of thumb opposition, abduction and ﬂexion, with preserved interossei. Reﬂexes were allpresent. There was subtle sensory loss over the thumb, index, middle and lateral half of the ring ﬁnger extending to the wrist. Flexion at thewrist appeared to bring on tingling and numbness within this area.
Clinically she appeared to have a right carpal tunnel syndrome.
Nerve conduction studies of the right hand showed:
Median motor latency5.5 milliseconds(<4.5)
Median sensory latency4.5 milliseconds(<3.5)
Diminished compound muscle action potential and sensory nerve action potential amplitudes.
An EMG showed ﬁbrillation potentials within the right abductor pollicis.
She was referred to orthopaedic surgery and offered an open carpal tunnel release and although it was explained that complications ofsurgery were rare with a 90% success rate, she declined this offer.
What might be a long term alternative treatment option for this patient?

A 35-year-old gentleman, who is an oﬃce worker, is admitted to hospital with fevers, rigors and right-sided ﬂank pain with a urine dipstickpositive for nitrites and leukocytes.
His pulse is 120, blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg and temperature is 38.2°C. He is on no regular medications.
Clinically, he is diagnosed with pyelonephritis and is commenced on intravenous antibiotics for a few days. There is no history of childhoodurinary tract infections renal calculi or previous surgical procedures.
His admission laboratory results reveal the following:
Haemoglobin140 g/L(130-180)
White cell count18 ×10/L (4-11)
C reactive protein130 mg/L(<2)
Creatinine90 µmol/L(60-110)
An ultrasound scan of the renal tract shows multiple cysts in both kidneys, characteristic of polycystic kidney disease. He makes a goodrecovery and is due to be discharged soon.
Having read about this condition, the patient asks about whether imaging of the brain is necessary to look for cerebral aneurysms. Thepatient has no history of headache or neurological symptoms, and there is no family history of stroke or aneurysms.
Which is the most appropriate management step?
options: MRA of the brain as an outpatient
No routine imaging is required at this stage
CT brain with intravenous contrast as an outpatient
explanation: It is estimated that up to 8% of patients with adult polycystic kidney disease have cerebral aneurysms.

A 17-year-old male presents with a one week history of progressive lower limb weakness, diﬃculty swallowing, and shortness of breath. Hedenied any history of trauma.
Examination reveals absent ankle and knee jerks with non-responsive planters and hypotonic weakness of grade 2 in both lower limbs.Sensation was intact.
Which of the following are the most relevant next steps for this man?
explanation:
This man has a rapidly progressive ﬂaccid paraparesis with normal sensation (including sensory level on the trunk) associated withdysphagia and dyspnoea, all which can be attributed to Guillain-Barré syndrome.
He is in danger of respiratory failure, so the appropriate next steps are:Performing FVC as a monitor of lung functionNerve conduction studies (including F waves for the proximal spinal root, looking for widespread demyelination)A lumbar puncture looking for albumin and cytological dissociation.
EMG has no diagnostic value.

A 23-year-old woman presents complaining of a 'droopy face' occurring over the last 24 hours.
Two weeks previously she had several days of headache and mild photophobia. The headache was of acute onset and moderately severe.Over the last week she has also noticed mild lower back discomfort and occasional tingling in the feet which she put down to the fact thatshe had 'pulled a muscle' when walking.Two months ago she had returned from a holiday in Thailand.
She takes the oral contraceptive pill. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day and consumes alcohol socially. She has a family history of migraine andher mother died of a 'brain haemorrhage'.
On examination, she looks well. Pulse 88 beats/min, BP 105/75 mmHg, temperature 37°C. On examination of her eyes, she has normalpupillary responses to light and a full range of eye movements. Fundoscopy is unremarkable. Corneal reﬂexes are present equally on bothsides. She has diﬃculty closing her left eye and it rolls it upwards in the attempt. When the cheeks are puffed, the left side balloons morethan the right.
The rest of the cranial nerve examination is unremarkable. Power is symmetrical in the upper and lower limbs and tone appears normal. Shehas absent reﬂexes throughout, even with reinforcement. Plantar responses are downgoing bilaterally. She is able to do ﬁnger to nose andheel to shin testing adequately. Sensory examination of light touch, pinprick and vibration sense are all normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Guillain-Barré syndrome is the most likely diagnosis due to the history of:lower back painsubjective sensory symptoms in the absence of objective signsleft lower motor neurone facial palsy, andabsent reﬂexes.
The time delay between the onset of facial weakness and the initial headache makes the diagnosis of a subarachnoid haemorrhage,cerebrovascular infarction or migraine extremely unlikely.

A 78-year-old man is admitted to hospital having developed abnormal movements of his left side. He has long-standing hypertension, well-controlled on atenolol, but has otherwise been healthy.
On examination of his central nervous system, he exhibits sudden, violent, involuntary ﬂinging movements of his left arm.
What treatment should be given?
explanation: The description given is that of a patient with hemiballismus; the lesion is in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

A 68-year-old lady presents to clinic with an irregular low frequency tremor of her right hand and ataxia. She describes noticing the tremortwo months ago when she was holding a cup of tea.
On examination she has an irregular low frequency tremor which is present at rest and when she holds her arms outstretched. She has ahistory of diabetes, hypertension. She is a smoker of 20 cigarettes a day and drinks three bottles of wine a week.
What is the most likely cause of her tremor?
explanation:
Holmes' tremor or rubral tremor is secondary to a lesion in the red nucleus and can occur following a stroke in this area. It classicallyproduces an irregular low frequency tremor which is a combination of a rest, postural and action tremor as described in this case.
It is described as a 'wing-beating' type of tremor and is most prominent when the affected person is active or is maintaining aparticular posture. Signs of ataxia and weakness can occur.
This lady has multiple risk factors for cerebrovascular disease including hypertension, diabetes, smoking and excess alcohol use.
Essential tremor typically presents as action tremor which can affect the person's ability to perform activities of daily living.
Cerebellar tremor is a slow intention tremor, occurring at the end of a purposeful movement such as touching a ﬁnger to the tip ofthe person's nose. This tremor may be accompanied by dysarthria, nystagmus, gait problems, and postural tremor of the trunk andneck.
Parkinsonian tremor is characteristically an asymmetrical resting tremor. The tremor is classically seen as a 'pill-rolling' action of thehands that may also affect the chin, lips, legs, and trunk, can be markedly increased by stress or emotions.
Physiological tremor is a postural tremor occurring in every normal individual. It is rarely visible to the eye and may be heightened bystrong emotion (such as anxiety or fear), physical exhaustion, hypoglycaemia, hyperthyroidism, heavy metal poisoning, stimulants,alcohol withdrawal, caffeine, or fever.

A 37-year-old chef was referred to a neurologist with progressive wasting and weakness of the right hand.
He had had the problem for several months and had noticed reduced dexterity and clumsiness using the hand whilst at work. In addition he had burnt his hands whilst cooking or smoking, and has been completely unaware of doing so. This had caused multiple sores over theﬁngertips of both hands; otherwise he has been well in himself. He had no known medical history, however did sustain a whiplash injury in arecent minor car accident.
He took no regular medication, smoked 30 cigarettes per day and had no family history of medical problems.
On examination he appeared well in himself. He had a right Horner's syndrome, however the rest of the cranial nerve examination wasnormal.
On examination of the upper limb, there was evidence of right dorsal interossei, hypothenar eminence, adductor pollicis brevis and forearmwasting. There were also multiple scars found over the ﬁngertips of both hands. Tone was asymmetrically depressed at the wrist and elbowbilaterally (R>L) and reﬂexes were bilaterally depressed.
On examination of power, handgrip and wrist ﬂexion/extension were asymmetrically weak (right>left). Upper body strength appearednormal.
There was no cerebellar dysfunction; however examination of sensation revealed reduced pain and temperature sensation affecting botharms and anterior/posterior chest wall.
Lower limb examination revealed increased tone symmetrically with pathologically brisk reﬂexes and extensor plantar responses bilaterally.Power, co-ordination and sensation were normal.
Chest examination was normal.
Full blood count and biochemical proﬁleNormal
Chest x ray Normal
Cervical spine x ray Normal
In light of the history and investigations so far, what is the likely diagnosis for this patient?

A 45-year-old lawyer presents to his GP after his family have expressed concerns regarding his behaviour.
He was found to have embezzled money at work purchasing items from the internet. He made inappropriate remarks to friends and his workhad deteriorated to the extent that he was eventually sacked from his job. His wife reported that he would just sit and watch TV and lostinterest in his hobbies. He began to snack excessively and gained a stone in weight in a month.
On formal testing he scored 28/30 on MMSE, however he failed tests on verbal ﬂuency.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Frontotemporal dementia is more common under the age of 65. It presents with changes in behaviour and loss of insight morecommonly than memory problems. Patients are disinhibited, apathetic and can be compulsive overeaters. They may have a normalMMSE, visuospatial and language function but they fail on tasks of verbal ﬂuency and executive function. 
Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia and presents with memory problems, diﬃculties with activities of dailyliving and behavioural changes.
Characteristic features of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) are ﬂuctuation of awareness from day-to-day, signs of parkinsonism andvisual hallucinations or delusions occur frequently.
Parkinson's disease dementia has a similar pathological process to DLB and both are associated with progressive cognitive declineand parkinsonism. The dementia associated with Parkinson's disease occurs more than a year after the development of the motorsymptoms of the disease.
Vascular dementia classically presents with periods of sudden decline and then stability with a stepwise progression. Patients have ahistory of stroke, hypertension or ischaemic heart disease.

A 24-year-old female presents with an eight weeks history of headaches, which have deteriorated over the last week.
She is aware of a frontal headache, which is constant in nature and unrelieved by paracetamol. These headaches have tended to be presentwhen she wakes in the morning and lately have been present all day. Over the last six months she also explains that she has gained morethan 7 kg in weight.
On examination, she is rather tearful, has a BMI of 32 kg/m but has no nuchal rigidity and neurological examination is normal except for
bilateral optic disc swelling on fundal examination. Her blood pressure is noted to be 122/88 mmHg and her temperature is 37°C. An MRIscan of her brain is normal and LP reveals an opening pressure of 30 cm H2O but normal CSF analysis.
What treatment would you offer this patient if she had progressive visual loss?
explanation:
Visual loss is the single threatening complication of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH).
Urgent LP shunt is the treatment of choice.
Optic nerve fenestration is an alternative.
There are no comparative studies between the two interventions.

A 40-year-old man with a long history of alcohol abuse is admitted with an acute illness, comprising headache, fever, meningism and ataxia.
MRI brain showed patchy high signal abnormality of the brain stem. CSF analysis showed polymorphonuclear pleocytosis and low glucose. he had failed to improve after three days of intravenous cefotaxime treatment.
What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Listeria meningitis should always be considered in patients with meningitis associated with brain stem involvement, and inimmunosuppressed patients. The treatment of choice is ampicillin with gentamicin added for synergy. Gentamicin may be stoppedafter a week if clinical improvement. 
Neutrophils usually predominate in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) in patients with bacterial meningitis. However, a lymphocytosis isseen in approximately 10% of patients. Lymphocytes may predominate in 30% of patients with meningitis caused by Gram negativebacilli, or in Listeria monocytogenes infection.
Note that this means that 70% of patients with Listeria meningitis will have a neutrophilic CSF.
A lymphocytic CSF predominates in TB and fungal meningitis.

A 67-year-old man was referred to neurology clinic complaining of excessive daytime drowsiness despite his sleep pattern being good. Hiswife who accompanied him to clinic said that at times during the day he could appear vague and drowsy and his attention span wouldﬂuctuate when responding to her.
In the last month he had also developed visual hallucinations. He was becoming increasingly slow at dressing and a walk to the shops thatwould have previously taken 10 minutes was now taking over half an hour.
He had a history of hypertension treated with bendroﬂumethiazide and a previous left-sided cerebrovascular accident with good recovery.He was a smoker and drank 10 units of alcohol per week.
On examination his blood pressure was 156/88 mmg, pulse was 48 beats per minute and regular and heart sounds were normal. Neckexamination revealed small goitre. Chest and abdominal examinations were both normal. Neurological examination revealed hypophoniaand an expressionless face. Mini mental state examination was 15/30 with deﬁciencies in verbal ﬂuency, executive function and visuospatialtesting. There were no abnormalities detected within the cranial nerves.
Peripheral nervous system examination revealed bradykinesia, increased tone bilaterally and unilaterally brisk reﬂexes on the left anddelayed relaxation on the right. Examination of the lower limb revealed a shuﬄing gait, and asymmetrically increased tone on the left. Theleft plantar response was extensor. No abnormalities could be detected within the sensory or cerebellar systems.
Investigations revealed:
Full blood countNormal
Biochemistry Normal
Thyroxine 50 nmol/L(58-174)
Thyroid stimulating hormone12 U/L(<4.5)
What is the best next step in the management of this patient?

An 80-year-old man presented to his GP having developed uncontrollable ﬂinging movements of his right arm and leg in the last few days.He had been previously well prior to the event.
The movements were irregular involving the proximal limb muscles and did not follow a particular pattern. They occurred several times aminute and had led to several falls. He had a past medical history of hypertension and ischaemic heart disease and took regular ramipril andaspirin.
He was a smoker of 10 cigarettes per day and did not drink any alcohol. There was no family history of neurological disease.
On examination he was alert and orientated, but had experienced several episodes of ﬂinging proximal movements of his right upper andlower limb, which made examination diﬃcult. Tone, power and reﬂexes all appeared normal and there were no obvious cranial nerveabnormalities. General examination revealed a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg, pulse of 78/min and regular and heart sounds were normal.
Investigations revealed:
Haemoglobin142 g/L(130-180)
White cell count6.7 ×10/L (4-11)
Platelets 235 ×10/L (150-400)
Serum sodium135 mmol/L(137-144)
Serum potassium4.5 mmol/L(3.5-4.9)
Serum urea 3.6 mmol/L(2.5-7.5)

Given the history and above ﬁndings, where is the probable location of the lesion?

A 34-year-old man presented to the Emergency department with a three day history of paraesthesia in his feet then hands. In the last 24hours he had noticed weakness of his thighs particularly when walking down stairs and also some weakness affecting his shoulders.
He had been well prior to this other than having a mild case of gastroenteritis thought to be due to a Chinese takeaway.
On examination he was somewhat anxious. Cranial nerve examination did not reveal any abnormalities and fundoscopy was entirely normal.On examination of the upper limb, tone was bilaterally reduced at both wrists and no reﬂexes could be elicited. Lower limb examinationrevealed 2/5 power. All reﬂexes were absent and sensation was reduced to all modalities affecting both feet.
A lumbar puncture was performed and yielded the following data:
Opening pressure14 cmH2O(5-18)
CSF protein 0.40 g/L(0.15-0.45)
CSF white cell count4 cells per ml(<5 cells)
CSF red cell count2 cells per ml(<5 cells)
CSF oligoclonal bandsNegative-
What is the diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: His symptoms and signs are compatible with an acute motor and sensory neuropathy following infection as in Guillain-Barrésyndrome. Paraesthesias in the hands and feet accompany the weakness in more than 80% of patients, but sensory abnormalitieson examination are frequently mild.

A 76-year-old male presents with visual loss.
Examination reveals a blood pressure of 168/102 mmHg and fundoscopy shows an embolus to right superior temporal branch of the retinalartery.
Carotid dopplers are arranged and these show normal left sided carotids, but 90% Right External Carotid Artery stenosis with approximately70% Right Internal Carotid Artery stenosis.
What would be the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
People with neurological symptoms following a stroke or TIA with a carotid stenosis of 50-99% according to some guidelines or 70-99% according to the ECST (European Carotid Surgery Trialists' Collaborative Group) criteria, should be assessed and referred forcarotid endarterectomy within 1 week of onset of stroke or TIA symptoms
If less than that aspirin and control of vascular risk factors is the treatment of choice. The loading dose of aspirin is 300 mg stat.
Further Reading:
NICE. Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s (CG68).

A 72-year-old woman is seen with a four month history of diﬃculty swallowing liquids. Her partner has noticed a change in her voice, it hasbecome quieter and less distinct. She feels that her problems have been progressive rather than ﬂuctuant. There is no past medical or drughistory.
On examination the pupils, fundoscopy and eye movements are normal. There is no evidence of a facial palsy, and hearing is intact in bothears. The tongue is not wasted, although you notice some fasciculations. The tongue, when protruded, deviates to the left. Palatal elevationon saying 'ah' reveals that the left side elevates normally, but the right side deviates towards the left (that is, midline). Sensory examination isentirely normal. Apart from a brisk jaw jerk, the rest of the examination is entirely normal.
Lumbar puncture reveals:
CSF protein0.1 g/L(0.15-0.45)
Cells One lymphocyte/mm
CSF glucose3.4 mmol/L(3.3-4.4)
Serum glucose5.6 mmol/L(3.0-6.0)
An MRI scan of the brain is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is essentially the differential diagnosis of a bulbar palsy.
The main feature of the presentation is a bulbar palsy, although brisk jaw jerk is unusual in this setting.
Myasthenia is unlikely in the absence of ﬂuctuating course and eye signs.

A 57-year-old woman presented in the Emergency department after a short episode of loss of consciousness.
Just prior to the event she had learned that her son was seriously injured in a road traﬃc accident.
There was no incontinence or tongue biting. The episode lasted for about a minute and she was not drowsy afterwards. She denied anyheadache, chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations. She has no past medical history of note and is on no medications.
On examination, pulse was 88 beats/min, BP 130/70 mmHg with no postural drop and oxygen saturation 99% on air. Cardiovascular andneurological examinations were unremarkable.
Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to perform ﬁrst?
explanation:
In the acute situation the ECG is the most useful test for classifying syncopal episodes into high risk and low risk categories.
High risk cases are those of abrupt onset occurring in patients older than 55 years who have a history of heart disease or abnormalECG.
Low risk patients are those who have no underlying diseases and a normal ECG.

A 34-year-old female patient presented with a four week history of bifrontal headache, decreasing visual acuity and walking diﬃculties. Therewas no signiﬁcant medical history.
On examination of cranial nerves there was bilateral VIth nerve palsy and fundoscopy revealed bilateral papilloedema. Visual acuity wasreduced and gait was ataxic.
Routine blood count revealed an elevated platelet count of 867 ×10/L. Haemoglobin, haematocrit, white cell count, iron store and
inﬂammatory markers were all normal. MRI brain showed cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with a small cerebellar haemorrhage.
What is the next best step in management of this patient?
options: Combination of plasma exchange and corticosteroids
explanation:
This clinical scenario describes the case of haemorrhagic cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) due to essential thrombocytosis.
Essential thrombocytosis (ET) is a chronic myeloproliferative disorder associated with sustained megakaryocyte proliferation,increasing the number of circulating platelets (above 450 ×10/L). It is associated with thrombosis and bleeding.
Thrombotic events may include:StrokeTransient ischaemic attacks (TIAs)Retinal artery or venous occlusionsCoronary artery ischaemiaMyocardial infarction (MI)Pulmonary embolismHepatic or portal vein thrombosisDeep vein thrombosis (DVT), andDigital ischaemia.

explanation:
Cerebral ischemia may be delayed as a result of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) or cerebral vasospasm. It is the most commoncause of death and disability following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). It may lead to death or permanent neurologicdeﬁcits in over 17-40% patients following SAH. The clinical diagnosis of DCI is made when the patient experiences an altered level ofconsciousness or a new focal neurologic deﬁcit following an initial bleed. Typically, the development of DCI starts on day 3 after theinitial SAH and is maximal at days 5-14, resolving on day 21. 
The calcium channel antagonist, nimodipine, has been shown to improve neurological outcome and the reduction of the incidenceof cerebral vasospasm. There is no statistical evidence from controlled studies for a beneﬁcial effect of triple-H therapy(hypertension, hypervolaemia, and haemodilution), or the individual components, on cerebral blood ﬂow (CBF) following SAH. Insome studies, hypertension is more effective in increasing CBF than hypervolaemia or haemodilution.
Secondary effects of SAH include increased intracranial pressure, destruction of brain tissue by intracerebral haemorrhage, tentorialshift, and brain herniation, all of which contribute to pathology. Patients often survive these complications but may deteriorate morethat 24 hours later from DCI. This can cause serious morbidity or death in up to 30% of patients with SAH. DCI may result fromangiographic vasospasm, cortical spreading ischaemia, arteriolar constriction, and thrombosis.
Treatment for DCI includes prophylactic administration of nimodipine and current neurointensive care.

Treatment includes withdrawal of the offending agent, reduction of bodytemperature with antipyretics. Dantrolene, bromocriptine or levodopa preparations may be beneﬁcial.
Serotonin syndrome is a differential diagnosis for NMS but the two can be easily distinguished on thorough history and examination.
NMS develops over days and weeks, whereas serotonin syndrome can develop over 24 hours. Serotonin syndrome developsneuromuscular hyperreactivity, (myoclonus, tremors, hyperreﬂexia) whereas NMS involves sluggish neuromuscular response(bradyreﬂexia, rigidity). Hyperreﬂexia and myoclonus are rare in NMS. Also resolution of NMS takes up to nine days whereas (usually)it takes less than 24 hours in serotonin syndrome.
Hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, leukocytosis, elevated CK, altered hepatic function and metabolic acidosis are common to severecases in both conditions, which is why a thorough history and physical examination are essential in order to differentiate betweenthe two.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman presented to the Emergency department with a sudden onset weakness and numbness affecting the left side of theface, arm and leg. She had been out shopping with a friend at the time when she had developed a typical migraine attack, shortly after theweakness and numbness came on. There was no disturbance of consciousness, vision or speech.
She had a past medical history of troublesome migraines associated with aura and had a previous episode of right arm weakness six monthsago, which had lasted 20 minutes before she recovered. She took regular pizotifen 1.5 mg and Maxalt melt and was also on the oralcontraceptive pill. There was a family history of migraine and strokes and her mother died in her 50s with dementia. She was a smoker of 10cigarettes per day and did not drink any alcohol.
On examination her blood pressure was 135/75 mmHg, pulse was 65/min and regular and heart sounds were normal. On cranial nerveexamination there was left facial asymmetry and weakness with reduced sensation over the left face extending to the vertex. Pupils andfundoscopy were all normal. Peripheral nervous system examination revealed mild left hemiparesis of 4/5 with hyper-reﬂexia and leftextensor plantar response. There was numbness to all modalities over the left arm and leg.
A MRI scan of the brain showed bilateral, multifocal, T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the deep white matter.
A lumbar puncture was performed and yielded the following data:
Opening pressure8 cmHO (6-18)
CSF protein 0.35 g/L(0.15-0.45)
CSF white cell count3 cells per mL( ≤ 5)
CSF red cell count2 cells per mL( ≤ 5)
CSF lactate 1.1 mmol/L(1-2)
CSF oligoclonal bandsNegative
Given the above history and clinical ﬁndings, how should this patient be further managed?

A 74-year-old woman describes feeling dizzy and sick when she gets out of bed in the morning. Her symptoms only last less than a minute.Her most recent complaint was a feeling of moving when she hung up her washing.Past medical history - hypertensionDrug history - amlodipine, bendroﬂumethiazide.
Neurological examination is unremarkable.
How would you make the diagnosis?
explanation:
This lady is describing vertigo and the history is typical for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).
The Dix -Hallpike manoeuvre is used to make the diagnosis of BPPV.
Epley and Semont are manoeuvres used in the treatment of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).
Lying and standing BP is used to diagnose postural hypotension.
An MRI will not be helpful in making the diagnosis.

stem:
You are asked to see a 40-year-old woman who has a six week history of episodes of 'the room spinning around' lasting several seconds. It istypically most severe when she is lying on her right side with the ear down. During these episodes she also has nausea. She denies anyproblems with hearing or tinnitus.
On examination, she has a rotatory nystagmus with an onset several seconds after the sudden assumption of her head in the right lateraldecubitus position using the Hallpike manoeuvre and which resolves after a minute or so.
Repeated positioning of the head in the precipitating position results in the attenuation of the nystagmus. No other abnormalities aredetected.
Audiometry investigation showed normal hearing.
What is this patient's likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is characterised by brief episodes of severe vertigo accompanied by nausea andvomiting. Symptoms are usually most severe in the lateral decubitus position with the affected ear down.
Episodic vertigo usually lasts for several weeks and then resolves spontaneously. Hearing loss is not a feature.
In contrast to positional nystagmus from a central cause, the nystagmus in BPV exhibits latency, fatigue and habituation.
Both central (eg, brainstem or cerebellum) and peripheral vestibular lesions can cause positional nystagmus and vertigo.Centralpositional nystagmus is usually static, in that the nystagmus persists as long as the head is kept in the provoking position. Positionalvertigo due to peripheral vestibular pathology is always transient. Observations of the direction of nystagmus, as well as features oflatency and fatigability, can help conﬁrm a peripheral localization and make imaging unnecessary.

stem:
A 50-year-old builder presented to his GP having developed some weakness of his right shoulder and arm.
He had noticed signiﬁcant problems lifting heavy weights above his head and more recently had noticed reduced hand grip and numbness.His symptoms had slowly come on following an accident whilst at work over two months ago when had had fallen from a plinth. He had apast medical history of hypertension and mild asthma, was a smoker of 20 cigarettes per day and drank 20 units of alcohol per week.
On examination there was winging of the right scapula. Neck movements were full. There was also some wasting of the dorsal interossei ofthe right hand. In addition, there was some wasting over the thenar eminence. Tone was reduced at the right biceps and wrist with absentbiceps, triceps and supinator jerks.
On examination of power, there was weakness of the right peri-scapular muscles, shoulder abduction, elbow ﬂexion and extension. Therewas also marked weakness of ﬁnger ﬂexion, extension and opposition of the thumb. Sensation appeared diminished over the thumb, rightmiddle, ring and little ﬁnger, extending over the medial and lateral aspect of the right forearm.
EMG and nerve conduction studies showed ﬁbrillation potentials affecting small muscles of the right hand with absent sensory nerve actionpotentials. Studies in the left arm were normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has a history and clinical ﬁndings in keeping with a diagnosis of traumatic brachial plexopathy with C5-T1 rootinvolvement. He has winged scapula and weakness affecting elbow ﬂexion/extension and small muscles of the hand and sensoryloss affecting dermatomes C6-T1.
The lesion is most likely in the plexus rather than nerve root, as the nerve conduction studies conﬁrm absent sensory nerve actionpotentials, pointing to a lesion that is distal to the dorsal root ganglion.
There is nothing in the clinical history to suggest anterior horn cell disease or a muscle dystrophy.

stem:
A 14-year-old girl presents with a seven day history of unsteadiness, diplopia, dizziness and drowsiness. Prior to that she has been well andhas achieved average performances at school.
She takes no medication and her last menstrual period was two weeks ago. Family history reveals that her mother has hypothyroidism andher father has a history of epilepsy.
On examination, she seems well but there is coarse nystagmus, dysarthria and a wide gait ataxia.
Investigations show a normal full blood count, renal function and liver function tests. Chest x ray is normal. Both CT and MRI brain are normal.Lumbar puncture shows normal pressure, cells, protein and glucose.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most likely explanation is phenytoin toxicity which she has surreptitiously taken from her father's medication.
MRI of brain and cerebrospinal ﬂuid will exclude multiple sclerosis (MS), meningitis and encephalitis.
The history is too rapid for Wilson's disease.

stem:
A 35-year-old female presents with an eight month history of feeling tired after mild exertion and has experienced diﬃculty with attention.She was given a diagnosis of ﬁbromyalgia but she did not notice any improvement despite graded exercise, and seeks further opinion.
On examination, she appears reasonably well, has a BMI of 29 and a blood pressure of 128/84 mmHg. She has right sided partial ptosis withnormal pupillary size and reaction, and a nasal speech, both of which deteriorate with sustained activity. Deep tendon reﬂexes were normalthroughout. Her anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody test was negative.
Choose the appropriate investigation to conﬁrm your clinical impression.
explanation:
This patient is likely to have acetylcholine receptor (AChR) Ab negative myasthenia gravis.
The differential would also include congenital myasthenic syndromes and Eaton-Lambert syndrome. The former are unlikely giventheir rarity and the patient's age. Similarly in Eaton-Lambert syndrome eye signs are unusual.
ACh receptor antibodies are negative in 15% of generalised myasthenia gravis; the picture is suggestive of myasthenia gravis (whichis much more common than the other two possibilities), so doing a tensilon test and repetitive (not conventional) electromyogram(EMG) are the most appropriate choices here.

stem:
A 60-year-old man presents to the accident and emergency department complaining of gradual onset of slurred speech over many months.
Examination reveals proximal muscle weakness that improves with repetition and a bulbar palsy. He is frail and emaciated.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lambert-Eaton syndrome is a paraneoplastic effect of some small cell lung cancers.
It presents with proximal muscle weakness which improves with repetition and can cause bulbar palsies. Demonstrating thepresence of a malignancy and detecting antibodies against the pre-synaptic calcium channels on the neuromuscular junction is keyto making the diagnosis.
Acute cerebrovascular events would present with an acute focal neurological defect and not have a gradual onset or improvementwith repetition.
Motor neurone disease may present with bulbar features but the lack of muscle fasciculation, distal muscle weakness andimprovement with repetition make this unlikely.
Myasthenia gravis presents with proximal muscle weakness that gets worse with repetition and autoantibodies are detected againstthe acetylcholine receptor.
Parkinson's disease may present with monotonous speech and bulbar symptoms however the lack of tremor and symptoms whichimprove with repetition make this unlikely.
Reference:1. Kumar P, Clark M. Kumar and Clark Clinical Medicine. 6th ed. London: Saunders; 2005.2. NICE Pathways. Stroke overview.

stem:
A 45-year-old man presented with diplopia, dysarthria and diﬃculty with swallowing.
Over the next few days he developed weakness of the upper and lower limbs. On day four he was unable to walk unaided. He denied anysensory symptoms or bladder disturbances. His previous medical history is unremarkable. He is a non-smoker, does not drink alcoholexcessively. He does not take any drugs.
On examination he was apyrexial. His general medical examination was normal. His higher mental function was unremarkable. There were nosigns of meningism. Cranial nerve examination showed bilateral dilated and ﬁxed pupils. He had binocular diplopia but no obviousophthalmoplegia. He was dysarthric with weak cough. His vital capacity was 3.15 standing and 2.00 lying ﬂat. He had lower motor neuronetetraparesis of power 3/5. He was hyporeﬂexic with normal sensation and was unable to walk unaided.
Investigations including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, serum calcium, thyroid function tests, autoantibodyscreen, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and serum C reactive protein were normal.
His electrocardiogram and chest radiograph were normal. A CT scan of his brain was normal, as were nerve conduction studies and anelectromyogram (EMG).
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The clinical presentation of descending weakness with autonomic dysfunction (ﬁxed dilated pupils) is typical of botulism.
It is a neuromuscular junction disorder and therefore nerve conduction studies and EMG are normal.
Repetitive nerve stimulation shows incremental responses, which is diagnostic of botulism.
Cerebrospinal ﬂuid analysis is usually normal.

stem:
A 76-year-old woman presents to hospital following a fall.
Her family think that she has slowed down and they are concerned because of problems with her memory over the last few months. Herdaughter tells you she has good days and bad days.
On talking to her she describes that she sometimes sees visions of small children and animals, but she is not bothered by this. Her brotherdied ﬁve years ago following a stroke.
Addenbrooke's examination revealed problems with visuospatial ability, perception and verbal ﬂuency. Examination of her upper limbsrevealed increased tone but was otherwise unremarkable.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Characteristic features of dementia with Lewy bodies are ﬂuctuation of awareness from day-to-day, signs of parkinsonism and visualhallucinations or delusions occur frequently. Falls are also common. They have pronounced visuoperceptual impairment.
Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia and presents with memory problems, diﬃculties with activities of dailyliving (ADLs) and behavioural changes.
Frontotemporal dementia is more common under the age of 65. It presents with changes in behaviour and loss of insight morecommonly than memory problems.
Parkinson's disease dementia has a similar pathological process to DLB and both are associated with progressive cognitive declineand parkinsonism. The dementia associated with Parkinson's disease occurs more than a year after the development of the motorsymptoms of the disease.

A 35-year-old woman with alcoholic cirrhosis is admitted with deteriorating confusion and deteriorating ascites.
On examination, she is mildly jaundiced, has a temperature of 37.5°C, is agitated and confused and has a ﬂapping tremor of the outstretchedhands. Abdominal examination reveals tense ascites.
Investigations reveal:
FBC Mild leucocytosis
Sodium 142 mmol/L(134-144)
Potassium 4.2 mmol/L(3.5 - 5.5)
Urea 4.4 mmol/L(3-8)
Creatinine 110 µmol/L(50-100)

AST 110 IU/L(5-40)

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

A 28-year-old female presents with a three month history of deteriorating coordination.
Examination reveals a blood pressure of 124/74 mmHg, and the only abnormalities of note are right sided dysdiadokinesis with nystagmusand a tendency to fall to the right. You also notice a number of café-au-lait spots.
Which of the potential causes below would NOT explain her lack of coordination?
explanation:
This patient appears to have developed features of cerebellar ataxia.
This, coupled with the skin changes, would suggest a diagnosis of neuroﬁbromatosis Type 2, a condition associated withhaemangiomas of the central nervous system (usually retina or cerebellum).
Although a pituitary tumour is a possible, it would not explain the ataxia.

stem:
A 75-year-old man presented with sudden onset of severe back pain and weakness in his legs. He had a past history of hypertension,controlled with bendroﬂumethiazide and atenolol. He also gave a twelve month history of diﬃculty in passing urine: this had manifested asdiﬃculty in starting micturition and having a slow stream of urine. On the day of admission to hospital he had not passed urine for overeighteen hours. Two hours prior to admission to hospital he developed severe weakness of his lower limbs.
Examination of the abdomen revealed a palpable mass arising from the pelvis. Cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal on neurologicalexamination. A sensory level was detected at T12. Power in the lower limbs was 2/5 bilaterally and both plantar responses were extensor.Digital rectal examination revealed an enlarged hard, irregularly shaped prostate gland with no central sulcus. An MRI of the spine showedspinal cord compression from a mass arising from the vertebral body at T12.
What is the next most appropriate immediate management?
explanation:
Spinal cord compression is an emergency. An urgent MRI spine is essential. The whole spine should be imaged because multiplebone metastases are possible.
The commonest tumours to cause spinal cord compression from bone metastases include:lungbreastprostaterenal and thyroid carcinoma, andlymphoma.
The most appropriate management will be immediate introduction of high-dose steroids: this has been shown to improve overalloutcome by reducing mass effect. An urgent neurosurgical review should also be sought.
Surgery is the best option for a single site of metastases and radiotherapy for multiple sites. Further imaging by radio-isotope bonescan will be required to determine whether there are any metastases at other bony sites.

stem:
A 74-year-old woman accompanied by her daughter was seen in general clinic with episodes of disorientation.
Her daughter had witnessed several of these episodes whereby one minute she could be having a conversation and then next minute shewould start asking 'where am I?' She would keep asking this question, but seemed fully aware of her surroundings, and was able to performtasks in the house and otherwise seemed fairly attentive. These episodes could go on for several hours. Her daughter was particularlyconcerned as these episodes seemed to post date the loss of her husband from cancer and she was aware that her mother had taken todrinking a moderate amount of alcohol. She had not lost any weight or complained of poor appetite or disturbed sleep.
She had a past medical history of hypertension and arthritis and took regular bendroﬂumethiazide and Arthrotec. She was a non-smoker anddrank approximately 15 units of alcohol per week.
On examination she seemed fully aware of her surroundings but appeared disorientated in time and place and kept asking 'where am I?'When the physician explained she was in hospital she acknowledged the answer, but within minutes was asking the same question. Thiscontinued throughout the consultation.
She was able to comply with physical examination which did not reveal any abnormalities within the cranial nerves or peripheral nervoussystem. General, cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were all normal.
Investigations revealed:
Full blood countNormal-
Biochemistry Normal-
Thyroxine 59 nmol/L(58-174)
Thyroid stimulating hormone6.9 U/L(<7)
An MRI scan of the brain showed mild generalised cerebral atrophy.
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 60-year old male presents with ﬁve days history of tingling of his ﬁngers and toes.
Over the last two days he noticed progressive weakness of his upper and lower limbs. On admission he is unable to ambulate unaided. Onexamination he has a tetraparesis, areﬂexia with ﬂexor plantar response.
CSF examination shows:
Red cells 0 -
White cells0 -
CSF glucose3.6 mmol/L(3.3-4.4)
Plasma glucose5.2 mmol/L(3.0-6.0)
CSF protein1.3 g/L(0.15-0.45)
What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Intravenous immunoglobulins (0.4 g/kg for ﬁve days) and plasma exchange are the treatment of choice in Guillain-Barré.
They improve the long term prognosis and have the same eﬃcacy.

stem:
A 50-year-old woman is referred to you with a year's history of personality change.
She has become loud, sexually ﬂirtatious and inappropriate in social situations. She has developed increasing diﬃculties with memory andabstract thinking, but with preservation of arithmetic ability. Speech is relatively preserved and there is no motor impairment.
Which anatomical region of the brain is affected most?
explanation:
Pick's disease is a rare form of dementia characterised by degeneration of the frontal and temporal lobes.
Presentations are of frontal or temporal lobe syndromes, depending on the location of maximal lobar atrophy. Patients with frontalatrophy present with early personality change. Predominant temporal lobe atrophy is associated with aphasia and semantic memoryimpairment.
Pathologically, Pick's disease is associated with Pick bodies which are argyrophilic inclusion bodies within the neuronal cytoplasm.EEG is relatively normal by contrast with Alzheimer's disease.
Further Reading:
National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. NINDS Frontotemporal Dementia Information Page.

stem:
A 70-year-old man presented with 12 months history of ﬂuctuating memory and agitation. He also complains of visual hallucinations. Hisfamily were concerned and had taken him to see his GP who had prescribed him haloperidol which he had been taking for the last twomonths but this was withdrawn recently as the patient became more unwell.
On examination, he had bilateral limb rigidity and bradykinesia, and a mild right-sided rest tremor. The rest of the neurological examinationwas normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Diffuse Lewy body disease is characterised by ﬂuctuating cognitive impairment, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
The patients are very sensitive to neuroleptics which therefore should be avoided.
The treatment of choice is rivastigmine, which improves both the visual hallucinations, and cognitive impairment.
Reference:1. McKeith I, Del Ser T, Spano P, et al. Eﬃcacy of rivastigmine in dementia with Lewy bodies: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled international study. Lancet. 2000;356:2031-6.

stem:
A 60-year-old man was brought to the Emergency department after a fall in his bathroom.
Seen immediately by his family, he was already picking himself up from the ﬂoor and said he was not injured. His wife felt that he wastransiently dazed.
On examination, he was alert, and no abnormalities were noted. His medical history included a history of hypertension for which he wastaking bendroﬂumethiazide 2.5 mg daily. He was discharged without any further intervention.
Two weeks later his wife brings the patient to see you because the dazed state has returned. Examination reveals a temperature of 36.7°C, apulse rate of 84 bpm regular, a blood pressure of 152/94 mm Hg. On questioning he is slightly slowed, being disoriented to time with somedeﬁcit in recent memory. The patient moves slowly, but power is normal. Neurologic examination shows slight hyperactivity of the tendonreﬂexes on the right with unclear plantar responses because of bilateral withdrawal.
Which of the following would you request?
explanation:
This patient probably has evidence of a right sided hemiparesis and together with the history of confusion and previous head injury adiagnosis of subdural haematoma should be suspected.
Consequently the most appropriate investigation would be CT head scan.
Particularly in the presence of focal neurology, a CT scan should be peformed before embarking upon a lumbar puncture.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman presented with a six month history of numbness and tingling over the left side of her face, and the right arm and leg.She denied any weakness of the arms or legs and did not complain of any bladder disturbances, headaches or visual problems.
The problem appeared to be intermittent. She had a past medical history of irritable bowel syndrome and chronic lower back pain. She wasunemployed, smoked 30 cigarettes per day and drank 20 units of alcohol per week. She lived at home with three children aged 9, 5 and 3years. She admitted that she occasionally used cocaine.
On examination, she was alert and orientated. On cranial nerve examination there was decreased pinprick sensation affecting the whole ofthe left side of her face including the angle of jaw. Scalp sensation was normal. The rest of the cranial nerves were normal. On peripheralnerve examination there was impaired pinprick and vibration sensation affecting the whole of the right arm and leg. Tone, power, reﬂexesand coordination were all normal.
An MRI scan of the brain with gadolinium contrast was normal. A lumbar puncture was performed and the following data obtained:
Opening pressure130 mm HO (50-180)
CSF protein 0.45 g/L(0.15-0.45)
CSF white cell count5 cells per ml( ≤ 5)
CSF red cell count2 cells per ml( ≤ 5)
CSF oligoclonal bandsPositive
Serum oligoclonal bandsPositive
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 35-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia presented following an overdose of his own medications. He became progressivelyconfused, ataxic, and febrile.
On examination there was increased tone in his limbs with lead-pipe rigidity. ECG revealed a sinus tachycardia. Head CT, lumbar puncture andseptic screen were negative.
Which drug may help this patient's condition?
explanation:
This patient has neuroleptic malignant syndrome following an overdose of his antipsychotic medication. Treatment is withdantrolene or bromocriptine.
Atenolol is a beta blocker which may improve the tachycardia but is not used in the treatment of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Fluphenazine is a typical antipsychotic and can cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
N-acetylcysteine is used in the treatment of paracetmol overdose.
Sinemet is co-careldopa and is used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease.

stem:
A 75-year-old man presents with a right total anterior circulation stroke. CT head shows a bleed in the left basal ganglia.
What is the most likely cause of the haemorrhage?
explanation:
The most common cause of an isolated deep intracerebral haemorrhage in the basal ganglia is hypertension.
All other answers can cause primary intracerebral haemorrhage but occur less commonly than hypertension especially in thecontext of a single deep haemorrhage in an elderly patient.

stem:
A 50-year-old man with learning diﬃculties is referred because of urinary incontinence. He lives alone. Over the last two months, he has beenﬁnding it increasingly diﬃcult to manage simple household tasks like making meals and cleaning. He claims his "concentration is not as goodas before." He had a son who died from complications of multiple sclerosis.
On examination, he is orientated in time, place and person. On memory testing, he was able to register information but was only able to recallnot more than three items out of six after ﬁve minutes. Long term memory was patchy. On testing serial 3s, he reached 25 after 30 seconds.His thought content was normal, but affect was labile. He was unable to interpret the true meaning of a proverb.
Cranial nerve examination was unremarkable, except for horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze bilaterally. Examination of the limbs revealedpast-pointing in the upper limbs, diﬃculty with heel-to-toe walking in the lower limbs, brisk deep tendon reﬂexes and extensor plantarresponses. Palmomental reﬂexes were present bilaterally.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The recent onset of memory diﬃculties, mild impairment of attention and concentration and the lack of ability to reason would bemore in keeping with Korsakoff's amnesic syndrome than Alzheimer's disease as the memory impairment would be more severe inthe latter.
In addition, the suggestion of retained features of acute Wernicke's encephalopathy, in particular ataxia and nystagmus, add supportto the diagnosis of Korsakoff's amnesic syndrome.
Thiamine is given in established cases to prevent progression of deﬁcits.

stem:
A 35-year-old woman was admitted to the Emergency department, having presented with an episode of loss of consciousness whilst in thesupermarket.
Her friend who accompanied her had witnessed the attack and described her as suddenly becoming anxious, breathing fast then suddenlydropping to the ﬂoor and shaking her arms and legs. On admission 30 minutes later, she was still shaking her limbs violently, had beenincontinent of urine but had not injured herself or bitten her tongue.
She had a past medical history of anxiety and depression, but did not take any regular medication. She was a smoker of 20 cigarettes per dayand drank 14 units of alcohol per week.
On examination, her blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg, pulse was 92 beats per minute and regular, temperature was 36.8°C and oxygensaturation was 99% on room air. Her eyes were tightly shut and impossible to open passively and she was violently shaking both arms andlegs. Plantar responses were ﬂexor.
Given the above history and clinical ﬁndings, what is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
The clinical presentation is typical of pseudoseizure (non-epileptic attack).
Violent shaking, resistance to passive eye opening and normal vital signs are useful indicators of pseudoseizures.
Urinary incontinence can also occur in pseudoseizures but tongue biting is rare.
Simple observation is the appropriate management in this case.
Pseudoseizures are commonly misdiagnosed as true seizures and treated inappropriately with anti-epileptic drugs.

stem:
A 21-year-old man, known to have epilepsy, was admitted to the Emergency department having had a series of tonic-clonic convulsions athome. His only prescribed medication was sodium valproate.
On examination, he was unconscious and having continuous seizures. He was placed into a lateral position to maintain his airway and 10L/min of oxygen was given via a high-ﬂow mask.
Intravenous access was secured and he was given intravenous lorazepam. Five minutes later he was still having seizures and a further bolusof lorazepam was given; a further dose was given after another ﬁve minutes because of continued seizures. The seizures appeared to havesettled when, 30 minutes later, he had another generalised convulsion.
Which of the following agents should be administered next?
explanation:
Management of status epilepticus:Protect airway.Give oxygen 10 L/min via high-ﬂow mask.Administer benzodiazepine iv or rectally. Lorazepam is preferred because of long duration of anti-epileptic effect. This iseffective in ~80% cases.If the patient does not respond, the regime may be repeated after 5-10 minutes using the same or a different benzodiazepine.If seizures recur or fail to respond after 30 minutes a parenteral anti-epileptic agent should be started.
Intravenous phenytoin is usually used and is given as a loading dose of 18 mg/kg. Adverse effects are common and include CNSdepression and cardiac arrhythmias.
Fosphenytoin, a disodium phosphate ester of phenytoin, has several advantages over phenytoin:it can be given IV or IM (phenytoin can only be given IV) and can be given at infusion rates three times faster than phenytointherapeutic levels are achieved within 10 minutes, andit has a lower incidence of adverse events than phenytoin.

stem:
A 60-year-old man diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease was reviewed in memory clinic.
In the past three months his cognitive function had declined. His wife, who had accompanied him, expressed that he was having diﬃcultiescarrying out simple tasks such as dressing and eating. She had also noticed a paucity of speech, but felt that his general personality remainedintact. He had also suffered bouts of nausea and diarrhoea.
He had been commenced on donepezil 10mg/day six months ago and for the ﬁrst three months had responded to treatment. He had noother past medical history and took no other regular medication. His wife was his primary carer.
On examination he had normal demeanour and interacted well throughout the examination. He scored 11/30 on mini-mental stateexamination with deﬁciencies in recall, visuospatial tasks, language and executive function. He exhibited marked dyspraxia on testingalternating hand movements. Examination of the cranial nerves appeared normal. Examination of the peripheral nervous system revealedbrisk lower limb reﬂexes with extensor plantar responses.
Given the above account, how would you manage this patient?
options: Remain on the same dose of donepezil and add in an anti-emetic
explanation:
This patient appears to have deteriorated over the preceding three months and is not responding to the donepezil at maximal doses.
NICE guidelines recommend discontinuation of cholinesterase inhibitors once the mini mental state examination has fallen below12.
Switching to an alternative cholinesterase inhibitor is unlikely to alter this patient's condition and would lead to gastrointestinal sideeffects.
The best option would be to withdraw donepezil and possibly consider memantine, which is licensed for use in moderate to severedementia. The new NICE draft guidelines, however, do not recommend its use because of lack of cost effectiveness.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a severe headache.
She reports that this has been getting steadily worse over a period of two to three months and is now also associated with blurred vision. Shehas a past history of depression: she attributes this and a feeling of low self-esteem to her weight problem and bad skin; but for the past fourmonths has tried to address these problems by joining Weight Watchers and starting treatment for her acne from her GP.
On examination she is overweight and has moderately severe acne. She is afebrile and there are no signs of nuchal rigidity. Oropharynx isbenign. Neurological examination is normal except for blurred disc margins bilaterally and a limited ability to abduct the left eye.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:

He was single, lived alone and worked as a ﬁnancial analyst. He smoked ﬁfteen cigarettesper day and drank thirty units of alcohol per week. He occasionally used cocaine.
On examination he had impaired adduction of the right eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye. Convergence was normal. The remainderof the neurological examination was normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The ﬁndings of impaired right eye adduction with nystagmus of the abducting eye would be consistent with right internuclearophthalmoplegia (INO).
The patient describes binocular horizontal diplopia. The site of lesion is in the medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons. Because theconvergence centre lies in the midbrain convergence is usually normal.
The commonest cause of unilateral INO in a young person in the United Kingdom is multiple sclerosis. Sensory symptoms lasting forweeks are also common in multiple sclerosis. The dissemination of neurological symptoms in time and place would be consistentwith a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.
The gradual onset of symptoms will make a diagnosis of brain stem stroke unlikely.
Myasthenia gravis can cause a pseudo-INO. However, it never produces sensory symptoms or signs.
Guillain-Barré syndrome will be unlikely because of the absence of loss of reﬂexes.

explanation:

A 41-year-old woman presented to hospital with a two day history of severe right side headache and loss of vision.
She had a past history of hypertension, for which she was taking bendroﬂumethiazide. There was a family history of 'thyroid problems'. Therewas a past history of intermittent headaches, though these were not regular. Her current headache was the worst she had ever experienced.
On examination she was agitated and distressed. Her temperature was 37.5°C, pulse 110 beats per minute and blood pressure 145/95mmHg. There was chemosis and proptosis of the right eye. Upward and downward gaze was paralysed; lateral gaze was preserved. The rightpupil was dilated and unresponsive to light. The left eye was normal. Fundoscopy showed bilateral papilloedema.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a syndrome of chemosis, proptosis and ophthalmoplegia. The usual cause is infection spreading fromthe face, orbit or paranasal sinuses.
Symptoms include:Periorbital/facial painConjunctival and periorbital oedemaProptosisPapilloedema Blindness, andCranial nerve palsies (III, IV, V1, (V2), VI).
Untreated, the infection may lead to subdural empyema, meningitis and infective arteritis of the cranial arteries. There is a slightlyhigher incidence in females (1.3:1) with a mean age of onset of 40 years.
Cluster headaches (migrainous neuralgia) is characterised by recurrent episodes lasting 15-180 minutes of severe unilateralperiorbital pain with autonomic features.

A 26-year-old male epileptic is admitted with temperature and rash.
Over the last one week a rash has developed and he has become increasingly ill. Recently he has had some problems with epileptic controland has commenced carbamazepine with valproate.
Examination reveals an unwell patient with a temperature of 39°C, a diffuse erythematous, painful rash with evidence of some lateral slidingof these erythematous areas on palpation.
There is also blistering and inﬂammation of the oral cavity.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient's presentation and clinical description suggests a diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) due to carbamazepinetherapy.
TEN is a severe mucocutaneous exfoliative disease with an uncertain pathogenesis and a high mortality rate.
It is diﬃcult to say whether it is another variant of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and treatment of both are similar.
It is often idiopathic but may be associated with:Viral infectionsLeukaemiaLymphoma, andDrugs (in particular sulphonamides and anticonvulsants).
The suggested association with carbamazipine in this case makes toxic shock syndrome due to Staph. aureus remote, which likepustular psoriasis would not be expected to affect the mucous membranes.

A 30-year-old mechanic presented to the Emergency department with vertigo, dysarthria, ataxia, nausea and vomiting.
In the preceding ﬁve hours he had developed a severe occipital pain, which started whilst working under a car. He denied any hearingimpairment or any visual disturbances. He had no past medical history and he did not take any prescribed medication. He was a smoker of 20cigarettes per day and drank 20 units of alcohol per week; however he denied any illicit drug abuse. There was a family history of stroke andhis mother had died of subarachnoid haemorrhage at the age of 43 years.
On examination he was pale and vomiting and complained of severe occipital head pain. Pulse was 80/min and regular, blood pressure was120/80 mmHg and temperature was 36.5°C. Heart sounds were normal. The pupils appeared sluggishly reactive to light and fundoscopy wasnormal.
On cranial nerve examination, he exhibited gaze-evoked nystagmus towards the right, and had a marked dysarthria. On peripheral nervoussystem examination, there was an intention tremor of the right arm. Tone, power, reﬂexes and sensation were all normal. On lower limbexamination he walked with an ataxic gait and appeared to be veering towards the right.
In view of the above ﬁndings, what is the likely diagnosis in this man?
explanation:
This patient presents with a classical history in keeping with extra-cranial vertebral artery dissection.
Dissection and cardioembolism are the commonest causes of stroke in young people (less than 40-years-old). The onset of severeoccipital pain usually caused by trivial trauma is a typical presentation for dissection.
Symptoms in keeping with ischaemia of posterior circulation occur (cerebellar, brainstem signs).
Extra-cranial carotid artery dissection presents with haematoma in the neck and possible compression of the sympathetic chainleading to an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome and cranial neuropathies particularly cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII.

On examination his Glasgow coma scale (GCS) score was 15/15 and his blood pressure was 142/95 mmHg. He had marked right sidedweakness grade 1/5 in upper and lower limbs with an extensor right plantar response. A CT scan of his head showed a left intracerebralfrontoparietal haematoma.
Two hours after his admission he remained stable.
What is the best management plan?
options: Neurosurgical referral for evacuation of haematoma
Intravenous beta blocker to control blood pressure
explanation:
There is no evidence of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) and therefore measures to reduce ICP (mannitol, sedation, assistedhyperventilation) are not appropriate currently. 
In patients with an intracerebral haemorrhage, intervention to control the blood pressure is required only when the systolic BPexceeds 170 mmHg. However, the INTERACT2 trial involving 2839 patients, looked at intensive reduction of blood pressure in thesepatients to less than 140 mmHg. This did not signiﬁcantly affect rates of death or major disability, but did signiﬁcantly improve overalhealth-related quality of life. 
Though it may be pertinent to discuss the case with the Neurosurgical team, there is no need for their intervention at this stage.Intervention is required only when the patient has an intermediate/reducing GCS or when there is a cerebellar haemorrhage.
The patient is stable with a normal GCS.
Observation is all that is required currently.

explanation:
The patient had a left middle cerebral artery stroke probable secondary to left carotid artery atherosclerosis.
Carotid endarterectomy is not indicated if stenosis is less than 70%.
Recent trial shows that the addition of clopidogrel to aspirin is of no beneﬁt and increases gastrointestinal side effects.
Thrombolysis is only considered within 4.5 hours of onset of symptoms.
Studies have shown that admission to a stroke unit improve the overall prognosis after a stroke.
