He had only a few superﬁcial scratches and contusions on his face, elbows and knees and a small haematoma on his forehead. The patient isfully oriented to time, place and person, with a GCS of 15. He is up and about and demands when he can leave hospital.
What course of management would you advise?
options: Admit the patient for observation and consciousness charting
Plain x ray skull and C-spine
Discharge home with advice to return if any deterioration
explanation:
NICE have issued clear guidelines on the management of Head injury (CG176).
In the following cases, NICE recommends a CT scan to evaluate cases of head injury:GCS less than 13 at any point since the injuryGCS equal to 13 or 14 at two hours after the injurySuspected open or depressed skull fractureAny sign of basal skull fracture (haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal ﬂuid otorrhoea, Battle's sign)Post traumatic seizureFocal neurological deﬁcitMore than one episode of vomiting, andAmnesia for greater than 30 minutes of events before impact.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy complains of several episodes of collapse. He describes the majority of these episodes occurring when he is laughing. Hestates that he loses the power in his legs and falls to the ground. He is alert throughout and recovers quickly. He also describes excessivedaytime sleepiness with episodes in the morning of being awake but being unable to move his body.
Examination is unremarkable.
A diagnosis of narcolepsy is made.
What is the ﬁrst line treatment for excessive daytime sleepiness?
explanation:
Narcolepsy is a rare condition which is characterised by excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, andcataplexy (sudden collapse triggered by emotion such as laughing or crying).
In 1999 modaﬁnil was approved for the treatment of excessive daytime sleepiness. 
There is no cure for narcolepsy.
Clomipramine, ﬂuoxetine and sertraline are used in the management of cataplexy.
Amphetamine based compounds such as dexamphetamine have been used to control excessive sleepiness but are used lesscommonly due to risks of addiction.

stem:
A 35-year-old man presented with confusion. He had been well earlier in the day and had gone to work as usual. At midday he collapsedcomplaining of a severe occipital headache. He had vomited several times and was agitated.
Neurological examination was unremarkable. In the emergency department he had a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure and was noted to have atemperature of 39°C. MRI showed an area of high signal in the left temporal lobe.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is HSV encephalitis which presents with fever, headache, vomiting, behavioural changes, confusion andseizures. MRI classically shows high signal in the temporal lobes.
Listeria meningitis affects immunosuppressed patients or patients at extremes of age. It can present with reduced conscious level,seizures and cranial nerve palsies.
Meningococcal meningitis presents with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting and fever.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage classically presents with a thunderclap headache and neck stiffness.
TB meningitis presents gradually with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting and fever. It occurs more commonly in thosewho are immunosuppressed, for example secondary to AIDS.

stem:
A 47-year-old man with advanced HIV disease presented with fever and obtundation. He has not attended his clinic appointments for severalyears and is not taking antiretroviral therapy.
A CT scan of his brain was normal. A lumbar puncture was performed; microscopy of his cerbrospinal ﬂuid is shown below.
What treatment should this patient receive?
explanation:
The slide is an India ink stain of CSF that shows typical yeast-like forms of Cryptococcus sp; the thick polysaccharide capsule ishighlighted against the darker backgound of black ink.
The history is characteristic of cryptococcal disease in AIDS.
Treatment is with amphotericin B and ﬂucytosine (5FC); patients then require lifetime suppression with ﬂuconazole.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman was admitted to the Emergency department complaining of diplopia and headaches.
She had started with the headache in the morning, which she described as generalised and throbbing in nature associated with somenausea. In the last two hours she had noticed pain and diplopia on looking to the right, and her left eyelid had started to droop. She had notnoticed any change in facial sensation, or any weakness in her arms or legs.
She had a past medical history of migraine and took occasional Imigran for persistent headaches. Otherwise she was ﬁt and well. She was asmoker of seven cigarettes per day and drank 16 units of alcohol per week.
On examination she was alert and orientated. Her blood pressure was 132/78 mmHg with no postural drop and pulse was 78/minute andregular. There was some mild nuchal rigidity. Fundoscopy did not reveal any abnormalities but there was evidence of photophobia.
Cranial nerve examination revealed a left oculomotor nerve palsy with left-sided ptosis and mydriasis. There was no evidence of chemosis orproptosis. The rest of the cranial nerves and visual ﬁelds appeared normal. There were no abnormalities detected in the peripheral nervoussystem.
Investigations revealed:
Haemoglobin134 g/L(115-165)
White cell count6.2 ×10/L (4-11)
Platelets 199 ×10/L (150-400)
Serum sodium139 mmol/L(137-144)
Serum potassium3.1 mmol/L(3.5-4.9)
Serum urea4.9 mmol/L(2.5-7.5)
Serum creatinine101 µmol/L(60-110)
C reactive protein10 mg/L(<10)
Given the clinical account, which investigation is likely to clinch the diagnosis?

A 70-year-old woman presents with paroxysmal dizziness where she has episodes where the room spins. These symptoms are exacerbatedwhen she rolls over in bed to the right and when she reaches above her head. There are no other symptoms.
Neurological and general medical examination is otherwise normal. The vertigo can be reproduced by turning the head of the patient 45degrees to the right and then taking the patient to the supine position. There is nystagmus (upbeating and torsional), which last only a fewseconds.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a typical history of benign positional vertigo.
It usually occurs on lying and turning the head to one side.
Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces the symptoms.

stem:
You are asked to see a 25-year old woman on the labour ward. She had a vaginal delivery of a baby boy who was severely hypotonic andrequired resuscitation and ventilation.
On examination she has bilateral ptosis, global weakness (more marked distally) and bilateral catacacts. She reports that her father also hadbilateral cataracts and died aged 58 years.
What is the mother's likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myotonic dystrophy (Steinert's disease) is the commonest adult muscular dystrophy.
Myotonia is often evident at an early age, but the severity is variable and many patients do not present until adulthood.
Distal weakness is often more marked than proximal weakness; there is a typical facial appearance due to atrophy of temporalis,masseter and facial muscles. Men often have frontal balding and some women also have hair loss. Cataracts are common.
Congenital myotonic dystrophy is a more severe form of the disease that occurs in children born to mothers who have establishedmyotonic dystrophy. Babies are hypotonic and frequently require assisted ventilation.
Galactosaemia seldom presents with problems at birth. Babies develop diarrhoea and fail to gain weight. Liver disease ensues unlessdiagnosed. Cataracts are common.
Myasthenia gravis frequently presents in the third or fourth decade of life and exacerbations are common in pregnancy. While thisrequires special attention for the mother, the baby is unaffected.
Similarly, Guillain-Barre syndrome would not affect the baby.

stem:
A 20-year-old woman has a history of paroxysmal episodes of dysarthria, ataxia and diplopia lasting for 20-30 minutes followed by right-sidedsevere headache associated with vomiting lasting for one to three days. The episodes occur once every month.
MRI brain and MR angiogram are normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is basilar migraine.
The normal MRI brain and MR angiogram exclude other possibilities.

stem:
A 35-year-old man was admitted to hospital having developed sudden onset quadriparesis, associated with complete loss of speech.
His partner who had been present at the time stated that he had been well and had not complained of any symptoms prior to the event. he had no past medical history and did not take any prescribed medications. He was however a frequent user of cocaine and occasionallyinjected heroin.
On admission he was found to have a Glasgow coma scale of 3/15 (V1, M1, E1). There was no nuchal rigidity or rash. His blood pressure was138/89 mmHg, pulse was 78 beats per minute and regular temperature was 36.8°C and blood glucose monitoring read a level of 5.6mmol/L.
General, cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. Neurological examination revealed pinpoint pupils with oculoparesis ofhorizontal movements on oculocephalic testing. Limb examination revealed generalised hypertonia and hyperreﬂexia with bilateral extensorplantar responses. He was intubated and taken to intensive care.
Over the next four weeks he was extensively investigated. He subsequently regained consciousness although was unable to speak andexhibited decerebrate rigidity. He could open his eyes and look up and down, but was unable to make any other purposeful response.
What is the most likely aetiology for this patient's condition?
options: Supratentorial mass with secondary brainstem compression
explanation:
This patient has developed 'locked in syndrome' most likely as a result of a pontine haemorrhage.
We are given the clue that he is a cocaine abuser, and pinpoint pupils together with sudden onset coma and quadriparesis place thelesion within the brainstem (pons).
The cerebral cortex is intact in 'locked in syndrome' and therefore the patient has awareness, but is unable to communicate verballyonly through eye closure or vertical eye movements.
A supratentorial mass with brainstem compression is likely to cause a crossed hemiparesis associated with third nerve palsy.
A venous sinus thrombosis can present with coma with or without focal signs and seizures. It would not explain pupillary changes.

stem:
You are referred a 35-year-old teacher who complains of episodes of severe unilateral orbital and temporal headaches lasting approximatelyﬁve minutes each and occurring 20-30 times a day. The headaches have been occurring daily for more than a year with no remission. Thepain is described as constant and boring.
During these episodes she also experiences mild nasal congestion and increased lacrimation.
Which of the following is the treatment of choice in this patient?
explanation:
The patient is suffering from chronic paroxysmal hemicrania which has features of cluster headaches but is associated with attacksof shorter duration and increased frequency.
In this condition, each headache can last between 3-45 minutes and occur 20-40 times per day.
In contrast, in episodic cluster headache, each headache lasts 15-180 minutes, occurs one to three times daily for four to eightweeks, with each cluster occurring several times yearly.
Chronic paroxysmal hemicrania almost invariably responds to indomethacin.
Further Reading:
Medscape: Chronic Paroxysmal Hemicrania.

stem:
A 76-year-old man presents with a two year history of poor memory, falls and worsening mobility. He also complains of distressing auditoryand visual hallucinations.
His medication consists of sinemet, aspirin, selegeline and ropinirole. He is unable to tolerate even small doses of neuroleptics, with markedcognitive deterioration, drowsiness and myoclonus. His past medical history includes diabetes mellitus and hypertension.
Examination reveals evidence of bradykinesia and cog-wheel rigidity. Postural hypotension is detected with a 15 mmHg drop in systolicblood pressure on standing. There is no evidence of opthalmoplegia. His mini-mental test score is 18/30.
CT head shows evidence of small vessel disease.
What is the most likely underlying disease?
explanation:
Dementia of Lewy body type accounts for 10-20% of cases of dementia.
Lewy bodies are intraneuronal, eosinophilic inclusion bodies found in cortical areas (they are also found in brainstem of patients withParkinson's disease). The main clues to the diagnosis are the characteristic severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions, and thepresence of hallucinations (and delusions).
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is less likely in view of presence of vascular risk factors. Hallucinations and delusions are also less likely inAD.
The postural hypotension is a red herring for autonomic dystrophy (intellect spared in Multiple system atrophy) as it is more likely tobe iatrogenic.
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in older people is rapidly fatal within a few months characterised by progressive multifocal neurologicaldysfunction (ataxia, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs, stroke, cerebellar syndrome) and dementia.

stem:
A 59-year-old man presented to his GP with wasting and weakness of the muscles in his left hand.
He had noticed severely impaired hand grip and had noticed problems with writing. He had also developed a tingling sensation over the palmof his hand extending up the forearm. Otherwise he felt well in himself and had not noticed any weakness or wasting of the right hand orlower limb. His weight was stable and he denied any neck problems or swallowing diﬃculties.
He had a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis and hypertension treated with bendroﬂumethiazide and ibuprofen. He was a smoker of10 cigarettes per day and consumed 4 units of alcohol per week.
On examination he appeared alert and orientated. Fundoscopy and cranial nerve examination were all normal and neck movements werefull. On examination of the upper limb, there was signiﬁcant wasting over the left thenar eminence and fasciculations with a small burn overthe left thumb. No other fasciculations could be detected in the proximal limb or other hand. Tone appeared normal and reﬂexes were intact.There was weakness of thumb abduction and opposition, with loss of pinprick and light touch sensation over the thumb, index and middleﬁnger. On examination of the lower limb, no abnormalities could be found.
Nerve conduction studies showed:Absent sensory action potential in median palmar branches.Denervation of the abductor pollicis brevis.Normal sensory and motor conduction studies in the right upper limb and lower limbs.
Given the above history and clinical ﬁndings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is the typical appearance of carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) arising as a result of pressure on the median nerve in the carpaltunnel.

A 47-year-old man with HIV disease presents to hospital with a tonic-clonic seizure.
He had initially presented six months previously with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia with a CD4 T lymphocyte count of 10 cells/mm and
had subsequently started on highly active antiretroviral therapy. His most recent CD4 count, taken one month prior to his new presentation,was 50 cells/mm.
On examination he has no focal weakness, but both plantar responses are extensor. Fundoscopy is normal.
A CT scan of his brain is shown.
What is the diagnosis?

A 21-year-old male is admitted with severe acute onset headache. He is disoriented and drowsy and has neck stiffness.
Investigations suggest a diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage.
What grade of illness does this patient have on the Hunt and Hess scale?
explanation:
This gentleman's history is suggestive of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH).
The Hunt and Hess scale grades SAH thus:1. Asymptomatic or minimal headache & slight neck stiffness2. Moderate or severe headache with neck stiffness, but no neurological deﬁcit other than cranial nerve palsy3. Drowsiness with confusion or mild focal neurology4. Stupor with moderate to severe hemiparesis or mild decerebrate rigidity5. Deeply comatose with severe decerebrate rigidity.
Severity and mortality increase with grade.
Reference:
Hunt WE, Hess RM. Surgical risk as related to time of intervention in the repair of intracranial aneurysms. J Neurosurg. 1968;28:14-20.

stem:
A 68-year-old female with metastatic breast cancer complains of back pain.
When you question her further, she also complains of pins and needles in her legs. The nursing staff inform you that she has developedurinary incontinence over the period of the last 12 hours.
Which of the following statements regarding this patient's management is correct?
options: High dose steroids should only be commenced when the diagnosis is conﬁrmed by MRI scan
Pre-treatment ambulatory function is the best determinant of post treatment gait function
Treatment for spinal cord compression is effective in approximately 10% of patients
An MRI of the spine is not indicated as she has known advanced cancer
explanation:
This is an oncological emergency. The earlier the diagnosis of spinal cord compression is made, the more likely it is that thetreatment will achieve a satisfactory outcome. Eighty per cent of patients will maintain mobility if ambulatory function is good atpresentation.
The deﬁnitive investigation in this case is an MRI of the vertebral column to look for vertebral collapse or other vertebral disease. 
Steroids should be commenced on clinical suspicion of spinal cord compression; diagnosis may be delayed, and steroid treatmentmay minimise permanent damage.
Urgent radiotherapy is the deﬁnitive treatment, although neurosurgical opinion should be sought in order to ensure that surgicaldecompression is not required. Treatment is effective in 90% of patients if the diagnosis is made early.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman presented to her GP with a left wrist drop.
She was unsure how it started but had noticed weakness of her wrist and ﬁngers for over a week. In addition, she also complained ofnumbness over the posterior aspect of the left forearm and dorsum of the left hand and had recently had some neck pain.
She had a history of depression and alcohol abuse and took regular ﬂuoxetine 20 mg/day. Otherwise, she was ﬁt and well and had no familyhistory of medical problems.
On examination of the upper limb, there was no apparent wasting or fasciculation. On examination of tone, there was slight reduction at theleft elbow and wrist. The biceps, triceps and supinator reﬂexes were also depressed in the left arm and normal in the right. On examination ofpower, there was weakness of left elbow extension, ﬂexion of the elbow with the forearm midway between pronation and supination,supination of the forearm, extension of the wrist and ﬁngers and extension and abduction of the thumb in the plane of the palm. Shoulderabduction appeared normal. Sensation was impaired over the posterior forearm and also the dorsum of the hand.
An MRI scan of the cervical spine showed mild degenerative disc disease affecting C5-C7.
Where will the lesion be on nerve conduction studies?
options: Motor neurone disease affecting C7 anterior horn cells
explanation:
This patient presents with a pattern of weakness and reﬂex changes in keeping with a radial nerve palsy, most likely around the spiralgroove. This often occurs as a result of Saturday night palsy, whereby an inebriated patient has caused pressure palsy.
This typically causes weakness of wrist and ﬁnger extension and also affects the supinator and brachioradialis (C5/6)
The reﬂexes are all depressed with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand, and posterior forearm. A C7 root lesion and a posteriorcord problem would not explain the involvement of supinator or brachioradialis (C5/6).
A posterior interosseous nerve lesion would cause weakness of the extensors of the wrist and ﬁngers only. This is extremely rare andmay occur as a result of compression at the radial tunnel as the nerve enters into the supinator muscle.

stem:
A 45-year-old left-handed man presents with sudden onset of headaches, dysphasia and left sided weakness.
Three months previously he had undergone debulking surgery for advanced carcinoma of the colon. Clinical examination revealed enlargedinguinal lymph nodes, hepatomegaly, left hemiparesis and expressive dysphasia.
Investigations showed a normal chest x ray. CT brain scan showed three small lesions throughout the cerebral hemispheres and one largehyperdense lesion in the right frontal region.
Which of the following would be the most appropriate in this patient?
explanation:
This patient has deﬁnitive multiple cerebral secondaries (the hyperdense lesion on CT suggests intratumoural bleed) and aggressiveprimary disease.
The extent of the disease excludes the need for further investigations.
The treatment of choice in this case is dexamethasone which must be started immediately, alongside proton pump inhibitor or anH2 antagonist to protect the stomach and bone protection.
Followed by this a staging CT is required and then discussion in an appropriate multi-disciplinary team setting.
Anticonvulsant prophylaxis is unnecessary if seizures are not a problem and are not effective in preventing ﬁrst seizures in patientswith newly diagnosed brain tumours.
Surgical resection is usually only recommended if a single cerebral lesion is found.

stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of limbic encephalitis?
explanation:
Paraneoplastic neurological syndromes are uncommon but important because they frequently present before the malignancy, andbecause they cause severe neurological disability. Examples of these are:Limbic encephalitisCerebellar degenerationOpsoclonus-myoclonusSensory neuronopathyLambert-Eaton myasthenic syndromeMyasthenia gravisDermatomyositis, andPolymyositis.
Acute to subacute onset of short term memory deﬁcits, with relative preservation of other cognitive functions, is characteristic oflimbic encephalitis. The memory deﬁcits may be noticed after several weeks of depression, personality change, or irritability.
Seizures can occur and are most often partial complex seizures. Olfactory and gustatory hallucinations are common.
Some patients also develop signs of diencephalic-hypothalamic dysfunction, including drowsiness, hyperthermia, hyperphagia, and,less frequently, pituitary hormonal deﬁcits.
In 60% of cases, limbic encephalitis is a paraneoplastic disorder and indicates the presence of an underlying cancer; the mostcommon underlying malignancy is small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC), followed by testicular cancer, thymoma, and Hodgkin'slymphoma.
In contrast to patients with other paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes, in whom magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is of limitedusefulness in helping to establish the diagnosis, patients with limbic encephalitis may present with early MRI changes suggestive ofthe disorder.

stem:
An 85-year-old lady is admitted from a nursing home with reduced GCS of 12. She had been complaining of a headache for two days prior toadmission and had become increasingly confused.
On admission, she is pyrexial and has a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure. Examination of her cardiorespiratory system is unremarkable but shehas evidence of neck stiffness and up-going planters.
CT head is normal.
Lumbar puncture shows an elevated CSF opening pressure.
CSF count is predominantly lymphocytes and Gram stain shows Gram-positive bacilli.
What is the most likely organism?
explanation:
Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive bacillus which affects immunosuppressed patients, or patients at extremes of age. It canpresent with reduced conscious level, seizures, and cranial nerve palsies. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) shows predominantly alymphocytosis with a normal glucose.
Bacterial meningitis caused by Haemophilus inﬂuenzae, Neisseria meningitides and Streptococcus pneumoniae has CSF whichshows a reduced glucose and predominantly polymorphs.
Haemophilus inﬂuenzae is a Gram-negative bacillus.
Neisseria meningitides is a Gram-negative coccus.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive coccus.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis has CSF which shows predominantly lymphocytes but the history is sub-acute onset and the organismis an acid and alcohol fast bacillus on Ziehl-Neelsen staining.

stem:
A 60-year-old woman presented with a three month history of diplopia and blurred vision of left eye. She denied any pain or otherneurological symptoms. Her previous medical history is unremarkable. She smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks alcohol in moderation.
Her general medical examination is normal. Her visual acuity on the right is 6/6 and on the left 6/36. There is left partial ptosis and mildproptosis with conjunctival injection. The left pupil is smaller than the right but reacting normally to light. There is some limitation ofabduction of the left eye. Fundoscopy showed a pale left optic disc. The left corneal reﬂex is reduced. The remainder of the neurologicalexamination is normal.
Routine blood tests including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function, serum calcium, serum creatinekinase, and autoantibody screen were normal. Her electrocardiogram and chest radiograph showed no abnormalities.
Slit lamp examination was normal and intraocular pressures were within normal range.
Where is the most likely site of the lesion causing her symptoms?
explanation:
The combination of optic neuropathy, proptosis, chemosis, Horner's syndrome, ophthalmoplegia (in this case due to sixth nervepalsy) and involvement of the ﬁrst branch of the trigeminal nerve is typical of orbital apex syndrome.
There is some disease process (causing the orbital apex syndrome) causing partial defects in the nerves. It is not the presence orabsence of function in a particular nerve that makes the diagnosis, it is the pattern of involvement.
Further Reading:
Yeh S, Foroozan R. Orbital apex syndrome. Curr Opin Ophthalmol. 2004;15:490-8.

stem:
A 60-year-old woman presented with a three month history of unsteadiness and fatigue. In her past medical history she was diagnosed withtype 2 diabetes mellitus four years ago, and one year ago had been diagnosed with hypothyroidism.
She was taking metformin 500 mg tds and thyroxine 100 µg daily. Her most recent thyroid function tests were normal.
On examination she had spastic paraparesis, absent knee and ankle reﬂexes, extensor plantar responses, absent joint position sense up toknees with normal pain sensation.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Subacute combined cord degeneration is due to vitamin B deﬁciency.
Pernicious anaemia is the commonest cause and is usually associated with other autoimmune diseases (for example,hypothyroidism and diabetes).
Prolonged metformin treatment has also been associated with B12 deﬁciency (in up to 10% of patients in a large four year clinicaltrial), therefore B12 levels should be screened every few years in patients taking long term metformin.
The combination of absent reﬂexes and extensor plantar response is typical and is due to co-existing peripheral neuropathy.
Dorsal column involvement with relative sparing of spinothalamic pathways is also typical.

stem:
A 17-year-old female presents with a progressive blurring in her vision over the last 12 months but denies any headache.
She takes no medication and denies use of illicit substances. Her past medical history was unremarkable and there was no family history ofnote. She neither smokes nor drinks alcohol.
On examination, her BMI is 32.3 kg/m and has a blood pressure of 120/68 mmHg. Neurological examination is unremarkable and on
fundoscopy she has bilateral blurred and heaped up optic discs which are obviously pale. Her CT head scan was reported as normal.
Select the appropriate investigation for this patient.
explanation:
The description of the pale but prominent optic discs goes with early secondary optic atrophy and hence should promote a searchfor a cause for a longstanding papilloedema.
Given the clinical scenario, the obesity and the 'normal' brain CT scan she is likely to have idiopathic intracranial hypertension; 10%of cases are free of headaches.
The next most appropriate investigations would be assessment for any underlying causes and include magnetic resonancevenography (MRV) (exclude cerebral sinus thrombosis) and cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) analysis with assessment of the openingpressure and other CSF parameters as a conﬁrmatory step.

stem:
A 28-year-old female was admitted to the neurology ward, having had double vision for the past several days and generalised muscleweakness. She had noticed that the weakness was particularly bad in the evenings and she was struggling to keep her eyes open.
She had also noticed some shortness of breath, which she had attributed to a recent cold. She had a past medical history of type 1 diabetes,and took regular insulin injections. She was a smoker of 10 cigarettes per day and did not drink any alcohol.
On examination she was noted to have bilateral ptosis and nasal speech. Her blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, pulse was 67/min andregular and oxygen saturation was 92% on room air. She was able to breath count to 10 and chest expansion was 4 cm. Her forced vitalcapacity was 1.23 l.
Cranial nerve examination revealed oculoparesis on the right lateral rectus and there was facial muscle weakness. Neck ﬂexion and extensionwere both weak. Upper limb examination revealed proximal weakness, which was fatigable, but tone, power, reﬂexes and sensation allappeared normal.
Lower limb examination revealed proximal weakness, normal tone but diminished ankle jerks with some evidence of impaired pinpricksensation of both feet. A short Tensilon test was positive and a plain chest x ray showed thymic enlargement.
Blood tests showed:
Acetylcholine antibodiesNegative-
MuSK antibodiesPositive -
Fasting plasma glucose17.5 mmol/L(3-6)
She was commenced on pyridostigmine 60 mg QDS; however her breathing and forced vital capacity deteriorated further.
What should be the next management step?

A 37-year-old man is admitted to the Intensive Care Unit following a severe head injury. He fulﬁls the criteria for brainstem death and holds avalid organ donor card. However, his family do not want his organs donated.
Which is the most appropriate action?
options: Discuss the case with the coroner
Discuss the issue with the transplant surgeon
explanation:
In the USA and Europe, only 50% of those who wish to donate organs following their death will have discussed the issue with theirfamily. The family are much more likely to consent to organ donation if these prior discussions have been made and the patientpossesses a valid donor card or is on the NHS Organ Donor Register.
If the family objects to the donation, healthcare professionals should discuss the matter tactfully and sensitively with them. Theyshould be encouraged to accept the dead person's wishes. Legally, they do not have the right to reject the patient's wishes, however,the ultimate decision rests with the family and it should be respected.
The most common reasons for relatives' refusal to consent to donation include:Did not want surgery to the bodyPatient had previously stated that they did not want to donatePatient "had been through enough"Family is divided over decisionUnsure if the patient had wanted to donate, andFear that the body would be disﬁgured.
The matter should not be discussed with the Transplant Surgeon, as he/she will have a conﬂict of interest.
There may be reasons why the coroner should be informed of the death of this patient but discussing this particular issue would beinappropriate at this stage.

stem:
A 60-year-old man presents with a two month history of progressive confusion, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence.
Examination reveals mild global cognitive dysfunction and gait ataxia.
CT brain shows enlarged ventricles with no evidence of obstruction to CSF outﬂow. Lumbar puncture reveals normal CSF pressure andconstituents.
Which one of the following managements steps is likely to be most helpful?
options: CSF drainage via repeated lumbar puncture
explanation:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with the triad of:DementiaGait disturbance andIncontinence.
It is associated with episodes of increased pressure related to impaired cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) absorption and therefore maybeneﬁt from CSF shunting.
Although the ventricular enlargement described in this case may derive from global atrophy and need not represent hydrocephalusthe other features of the case strongly point to the diagnosis.
In equivocal cases therapeutic CSF drainage via lumbar puncture is performed to identify the patients likely to beneﬁt frompermanent drainage.
Intracranial pressure monitoring to demonstrate the episodes of increased pressure is a more invasive alternative.

stem:
You are referred a 40-year-old woman with wasting and weakness involving initially the lower limbs and now the upper limbs.
She was unsteady and clumsy, especially in the dark. Her feet had also become numb. The symptoms have been slowly progressive over 10years. She had no bladder symptoms. She had no contact with her father, although she has been told he had similar features, albeit lessmarked.
On examination, tone was ﬂaccid and distal muscles in the legs were weak, especially in dorsiﬂexion and eversion of the ankles. There wasmilder weakness of the arms. Tendon reﬂexes were absent and mild blunting to pinprick was noted over the feet bilaterally. Cranial nerveexamination was unremarkable.
Which of the following is the most important steps to be taken in the investigation of this patient?
options: Measure immunoglobulin A levels and if satisfactory commence intravenous immunoglobulin treatment
explanation:
A logical approach to the assessment of such patients is essential and can be organised into a number of basic questions. Theneurologist faced with a patient with a neuropathy has to deal with literally thousands of possible causes, many extremelyuncommon, and these can only be simpliﬁed by deﬁning the neuropathy by other features that lead to the select few of most likelydiagnoses.
Mixed motor and sensory symptoms, slowly progressing initially in the lower limbs and then to the upper limbs, together with afamily history suggests a diagnosis of hereditary motor sensory neuropathy (HMSN). 
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies may distinguish between the demyelinating (type 1) and axonal (type 2) forms.
Genetic testing is available for certain types of HMSN. Genetic testing usually reveals the diagnosis and EMG and NCS helpdistinguish between the types.
Then the next step is neurophysiology - this will give information about whether this could be a central or root disorder and point todemyelination.It is less invasive than muscle biopsy (or nerve biopsy) and we do know suﬃcient information to commence treatment with beta

A 22-year-old female presents with an eight weeks history of headaches, which have deteriorated over the last week.
She is aware of a frontal headache, which is constant in nature and unrelieved by paracetamol. These headaches have tended to be presentwhen she wakes in the morning and lately have been present all day. Over the last six months she also explains that she has gained morethan 7 kg in weight.
On examination, she is rather tearful, has a BMI of 32 kg/m but has no nuchal rigidity and neurological examination is normal except for
bilateral optic disc swelling on fundal examination. Her blood pressure is noted to be 122/88 mmHg and her temperature is 37°C.
Which of the following is the single best investigation to make the diagnosis?
explanation:
The history suggests benign intracranial hypertension (BIH) and LP is diagnostic.
However, brain imaging will be needed to exclude a space occupying lesion, hydrocephalus and cerebral venous thrombosis.
MRI brain is better than CT brain to look for cerebral venous thrombosis where a 'pyramidal' defect in venous ﬂow is noted.

A 24-year-old man presents with sudden onset right sided neck pain, with pain behind his right eye.
Twelve hours later he develops right ptosis and miosis of his right pupil, with left sided weakness and facial droop.
What is the most likely cause of his stroke?
explanation:
Carotid artery dissection can occur spontaneously and is a common cause of young stroke (age less than 40). It typically presentswith neck, facial or head pain, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (miosis and ptosis) and contralateral weakness.
Cardiac embolism is a common cause of young stroke but is less likely in the presence of facial and neck pain.
Migraine with aura can cause stroke but commonly with posterior circulation symptoms and signs.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage classically presents with a thunderclap headache and neck stiffness.
Vertebral artery dissection causes head and neck pain but presents with posterior circulation symptoms and signs.

A 50-year-old man presents with tingling in the left upper limb. The pain originated in the neck and radiated down the left arm. He proceededto have numbness and paraesthesia in the left lower limb.
On examination he had restriction of neck movements and there was a mild wasting to be noted in the left biceps. There was inversion of thesupinator and biceps jerks. His knee jerk and ankle jerk were hyperreactive and he has a positive extensor plantar response.
He then developed paraesthesia and numbness of the right lower limb. A diagnosis of cord compression was made and he underwent asurgical decompression.
Post-surgery was complicated by septicaemia and urinary tract infection and he remained in bed for four days. He subsequently developedinability to dorsiﬂex his right foot and right big toe. There was numbness on the outside of the foot and there was decreased eversion, butinversion was normal. His reﬂexes remained as before.
What is the cause of the post operative weakness?
options: Recurrence of the original cord compression
explanation:
The commonest cause of acute foot drop after prolonged bed rest is entrapment common peroneal neuropathy at the neck ofﬁbula. Whilst it is possible for this to develop at the time of surgery, the complicated postoperative course in this gentleman is likelyto have contributed.
Typically there is weakness of ankle dorsiﬂexion, eversion, diminished sensation of the lateral aspect of leg and dorsum of foot.
The ankle reﬂex remains intact.

A 76-year-old woman presents to hospital following a fall. Her family think that she has slowed down and they are concerned because ofproblems with her memory over the last few months. Her daughter tells you she has good days and bad days.
On talking to her she describes she sometimes sees visions of small children and animals, but she is not bothered by this. Her brother diedﬁve years ago following a stroke.
Addenbrooke's examination revealed problems with visuospatial ability, perception and verbal ﬂuency. Examination of her upper limbsrevealed increased tone but was otherwise unremarkable.
What is the best evidence based treatment for her dementia?
explanation:
Rivastigmine is effective in treating cognitive decline in dementia with Lewy bodies. It may be effective in reducing anxiety, apathyand hallucinations; it has been shown to be better than placebo in LBD and for hallucinations.
Donepezil and galantamine are used in the treatment of Alzheimer's dementia.
Gingko biloba is a herbal medication which has not been proven to be of beneﬁt in treatment or prevention of dementia.
Memantine is used only in moderately severe to severe Alzheimer's dementia. It is usually started at 5mg and increased in steps of5mg every week until 20mg dose. 
Further Reading:1. Cummings J, Emre M, Aarsland D, et al. Effects of rivastigmine in Alzheimer's disease patients with and without hallucinations. JAlzheimers Dis. 2010;20:301-11.2. McKeith I, Del Ser T, Spano P, et al. Eﬃcacy of rivastigmine in dementia with Lewy bodies: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled international study. Lancet. 2000;356:2031-6.

A 45-year-old woman presented to her GP complaining of tingling in the right palm and right wrist pain.
She had experienced these symptoms intermittently however recently they had been keeping her awake all night. She had noticed areduction in grip and was struggling to work on the checkout counter at her local supermarket. Otherwise she felt well in herself and had notnoticed any weakness in the other hand or lower limb.
Her weight was stable and she denied any neck problems or swallowing diﬃculties. She had a past medical history of hypothyroidism andhypertension and took regular thyroxine, bendroﬂumethiazide and ibuprofen. She was a non-smoker and rarely drank alcohol.
On examination she appeared alert and orientated. Fundoscopy and cranial nerve examination were all normal and neck movements werefull.
On examination of the upper limb, there was wasting over the right thenar eminence and fasciculations with a small burn over the right indexﬁnger. No other fasciculations could be detected in the proximal limb or other hand. Tone appeared normal and reﬂexes were intact. Therewas weakness of thumb abduction and opposition, with loss of pinprick and light touch sensation over the thumb, index and middle ﬁnger inthe right hand. On examination of the lower limb, no abnormalities could be found.
Nerve conduction studies showed absent sensory action potential in right median palmar branches and denervation of the right abductorpollicis brevis. Sensory and motor conduction studies in the left upper limb and lower limbs were normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The history is in keeping with carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) arising as a result of pressure on the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.
The median nerve supplies the muscles of the thenar eminence: the abductor pollicis (C7, C8), ﬂexor pollicis brevis and opponenspollicis, and the lateral two lumbricals. The nerve conduction studies conﬁrm marked denervation and absent sensory potentialswithin the median nerve territory.
CTS is associated with hypothyroidism, pregnancy, amyloidosis and rheumatoid arthritis.

A 35-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant and who is known to have pregnancy induced hypertension is admitted to the EmergencyDepartment following headaches and a seizure at home.
On arrival, GCS is 9/15 and she has neurological signs consistent with an intracerebral bleed. Blood pressure is 195/85 mmHg.
What is the most appropriate immediate course of action?
explanation:
This woman has severe pre-eclampsia with a likely either and intracerebral bleed or cerebral oedema. The most important initialtherapy is to control any further seizures and control her blood pressure - intravenous magnesium is the therapy of choice.
She is likely to need intubation and controlled ventilation. She may require further measures to obtund the pressor response tolaryngoscopy.

A 51-year-old man was referred to the acute medical intake with a two week history of severe pain around his right eye.
The pain had started without any apparent precipitating event and had woken him from his sleep. He described the pain as severe and'boring' and radiated upwards over the right frontal and temporal region. The pain was not constant, but seemed to start every evening andpersist for periods of 20 minutes to over an hour. The headaches were associated with watering of his right eye and a blocked left nostril.There was no past history of similar episodes and no other past history of note.
On examination he was alert and orientated with a Glasgow coma scale score of 15/15. His blood pressure was 125/75 mmHg. He wasafebrile and there was no neck stiffness. The right eye was red with conjunctival injection and mild oedema of the eyelid. There was a partialright sided ptosis and miosis.
Which of the following therapeutic options is most likely to alleviate his symptoms?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is cluster headache (migrainous neuralgia).
This is characterised by recurrent episodes lasting 15-180 minutes of unilateral periorbital pain with associated autonomic features.Cluster headaches can occur at any age, but are most common in age 20-50 years; there is a strong male preponderance (10:1).
The pain is described as severe and boring and radiates up over the frontotemporal region and/or down to the jaw, neck or shoulder.There is frequently accompanying miosis with or without a Horner's syndrome. The ipsilateral eye is often red and watery; there isoften associated rhinorrhoea or a blocked ipsilateral nostril.
Oxygen 100% (6-8 L/min) often provides relief within 10 minutes.
Sumatriptan may also be used in the acute attack. Ergotamine, methysergide, verapamil and prednisolone have been used asprophylaxis once the acute attack has resolved.

A 45-year-old labourer is referred with a three month history of tingling and paraesthesia of the left hand.
On two occasions he dropped his cup of tea but put these down to a bit of clumsiness. His symptoms tend to be more noticeable in theevenings when he is resting or watching TV. He denies any muscle twitching.
Bladder and bowel function are reported as normal. Past medical history is unremarkable and he has not been involved in any accidentsrecently. His job means that he often has to use vibrating tools and do heavy manual lifting.
On examination, he has no obvious loss of muscle bulk in his upper limbs. Tone is normal. Power appears normal in all muscle groups. Apartfrom an absent triceps reﬂex on the left, his reﬂexes are all present and symmetrical. Sensory examination reveals loss of pinprick sensationon the palmar aspect of the index, middle and ring ﬁngers of the left hand. Tapping of the palmar aspect of the wrist fails to elicit any tinglingsensations in the hand distally. Joint position sense and vibration sense are both normal. Cranial nerve examination is unremarkable.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The sensory disturbance in the C7 dermatome and the absent triceps reﬂex (C7, C8) makes a C7 root neuropathy the best answer.
In carpal tunnel syndrome, the sensory disturbance involves the thumb, index, the middle ﬁngers and the lateral half of the ringﬁnger, and the triceps reﬂex will not be affected.
Erb's palsy is usually the result of traumatic avulsion of the C5 and C6 roots (commonly occurring during delivery at birth) and causesloss of shoulder abduction and elbow ﬂexion with loss of biceps and brachioradialis reﬂexes.
Klumpke's palsy, often the result of a fall that has been stopped by grasping a ﬁxed object with one hand, involves the C8 and T1roots and causes weakness of small muscles of the hand and of the long ﬁnger ﬂexors and extensors, and a sensory disturbanceaffecting the medial half of the ring ﬁnger and little ﬁnger.
A medial cord lesion also affects the C8 and T1 roots.

explanation:

His wife also says that he has never kept his gambling secret from her, whereasnow he seems to be concealing his actions.

His mood can be a little bit variable but this is nothing new as hehas always been frustrated by his diagnosis and the physical symptoms of the disease. His sleep is OK and he is eating well. 
He is prescribed levodopa and carbidopa as a combination treatment (co-careldopa) and ropinirole.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this problem?
explanation:
Impulsive and compulsive behaviour is an uncommon but important possible side effect of some anti-Parkinsonian medication.
Parkinson's UK have a useful information pack on this issue which is worth a read.
Patients started on levodopa or a dopamine agonist should be warned of this potential problem so that they are their family/carerscan monitor for any suspicious behaviour.
Further reading:
Impulsive and compulsive behaviour in Parkinson's

The nurses on the neurology ward asked the senior house oﬃcer to review a patient who had developed a fever.
The patient was a 42-year-old man who had been on the ward for several months and had a long term urinary catheter in situ. The patient'sneurological status was unchanged since admission, but he was not able to give any history.
On examination, the patient was lying in bed and was awake. He was febrile 37.5°C. He appeared comfortable with a respiratory rate of 12 perminute and pulse 75 beats per minute, regular. Blood pressure 120/75 mmHg.
His pupils were reactive to light, but the patient could not track a moving object - eye movements appeared to be random. He did notrespond to verbal commands, though he could move all four limbs spontaneously but with no clear purpose. He did not respond to anyverbal or tactile stimuli but pressure on the nail bed elicited a ﬂexor response. Both plantar responses were extensor. The patient mademoaning noises but there was no coherent speech. On occasions the patient laughed spontaneously - but not for any speciﬁc reason. Thenurses reported that he had a normal sleep cycle and that he was fed by a gastrostomy feeding tube.
Urinalysis showed the presence of white cells, protein and nitrites and microscopy revealed Gram negative rods.
What is the neurological diagnosis?
explanation:
Permanent vegetative state (PVS) is deﬁned as a state of 'wakefulness without awareness'.
The patient breathes spontaneously without mechanical support, is haemodynamically stable and has cycles of eye closure andopening that resemble a normal sleeping pattern but the patient is inattentive and unaware of his/her surroundings. Patients mayhave spontaneous movements (moaning, grunting, teeth grinding, roving eye movements) and may also smile, laugh and crywithout any apparent reason. Although there may be eye movement, the eyes do not track a moving object. Patients may respondto painful stimuli and may have myoclonus in response to startling stimuli. Primitive reﬂexes may be present. Posture may becomedecorticate and plantar responses are commonly extensor.

A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency department with a history of epilepsy.
He starts to experience jerking movements of the angle left of his mouth and then progresses to having jerking movements of his left thumband index ﬁnger. Finally, his entire left side develops jerking movements which subside in ten minutes.
After this he has a weakness down the left side for several hours. During the event he had full consciousness.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A jacksonian seizure is also known as a focal (partial) motor seizure. In this condition an uncontrolled, spontaneous discharge ofelectricity from one motor cortex presents with contralateral motor signs. The patient has preserved consciousness as it is a partialseizure and after the seizure it is common to have a Todd's paralysis where the limb is weak.
Temporal lobe epilepsy presents with the sensation of déjà vu or an unreal feeling and can progress to hallucinations and alteredconscious level.
Myoclonic seizures present with isolated muscle jerking.
In a grand mal seizure the electrical activity is throughout the cortex and consciousness is impaired and the patient maydemonstrate tonic-clonic movements in all their limbs.
Reference:
Kumar P, Clark M. Kumar and Clark Clinical Medicine. 6th ed. London: Saunders; 2005.

He had a past history of hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia and took regular atenolol and simvastatin. He was a smoker of 20cigarettes per day and drank approximately 20 units of alcohol per week. He was a builder and was married with two adult children.
On examination he was alert and orientated. His blood pressure was 150/78 mmHg taken in the right arm and 120/67 mmHg in the left arm.His pulse was 80/minute and regular and there was evidence of bilateral carotid bruits. Heart sounds were normal and his chest was clear.
On examination of the neurological system, tone appeared normal, reﬂexes were depressed at the biceps and brachioradialis with a brisktriceps jerk. There was no demonstrable weakness, however there was some impaired pinprick sensation over the thumb, and middle ﬁngerin the left hand. There were no signs of atrophy or fasciculations. explanation:
This patient presents with a classic history of subclavian steal syndrome brought on by exercising of his left hand, and associatedwith a reduction in blood pressure in the left arm.
Subclavian steal syndrome occurs when there is an occlusion proximal to the origin of the left vertebral artery. As a result blood isstolen from the right vertebral artery with resultant basilar insuﬃciency.

A 50-year-old man with learning diﬃculties is referred because of urinary incontinence. He lives alone.
Over the last two months, he has been ﬁnding it increasingly diﬃcult to manage simple household tasks like making meals and cleaning. Heclaims his 'concentration is not as good as before.' He had a son who died from complications of multiple sclerosis.
On examination, he is orientated in time, place and person. On memory testing, he was able to register information but was only able to recallnot more than three items out of six after ﬁve minutes. Long term memory was patchy. On testing serial 3s, he reached 25 after 30 seconds.His thought content was normal, but affect was labile. He was unable to interpret the true meaning of a proverb.
Cranial nerve examination was unremarkable, except for horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze bilaterally. Examination of the limbs revealedpast-pointing in the upper limbs, diﬃculty with heel to toe walking in the lower limbs, brisk deep tendon reﬂexes and extensor plantarresponses. Palmomental reﬂexes were present bilaterally.
What treatment would you initiate in this patient?
explanation:
The recent onset of memory diﬃculties, mild impairment of attention and concentration and the lack of ability to reason would bemore in keeping with Korsakoff's amnestic syndrome than Alzheimer's disease as the memory impairment would be more severe inthe latter.
In addition, the suggestion of retained features of acute Wernicke's encephalopathy, in particular ataxia and nystagmus, add supportto the diagnosis of Korsakoff's amnestic syndrome.
Thiamine is given in established cases to prevent progression of deﬁcits.

A 45-year-old man presented to the Emergency department with bifrontal headache and nausea which he had had for many weeks.
The pain had steadily worsened over the last 48 hours and he had vomited several times. He had also noticed marked deterioration in hismental capacity. His wife had accompanied him and said he was mentally slowed, easily distractable and his walking had deteriorated.
He had a past medical history of hypertension and took regular bendroﬂumethiazide. He was a non-smoker and drank 10 units of alcohol perweek.
On examination he appeared easily distractable and there was marked perseveration. On cranial nerve examination his pupils were meioticand fundoscopy revealed bilateral papilloedema. Ocular movements were full and the rest of the cranial nerves were normal. On examinationof the upper limb he had bilateral palmomental reﬂexes, but tone, power and reﬂexes were all intact. Lower limb examination revealednormal tone, power, reﬂexes and sensation, but he walked with a somewhat ataxic gait.
A CT scan of the brain showed dilated lateral ventricles with normal-sized third and fourth ventricles.
What is the likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
options: Tumour at the foramen of Monro
explanation:
There is obstruction between the lateral ventricles and third ventricle, as evidenced by the CT scan images.
The connection between these sites is via the foramen of Monro, which may be blocked by tumour or can be affected by horizontalshift from an expanding unilateral mass.
Dandy-Walker syndrome is a congenital failure of opening of the foramina of Luschka and Magendie, resulting in dilatation of theentire ventricular system.
The Sylvian aqueduct is the connection between the third and fourth ventricles and if obstructed would cause dilatation of bothlateral and third ventricles.

A 62-year-old woman is referred with a three month history of increasing weakness affecting the left more than the right arm. She alsocomplains of tingling and numbness affecting the left thumb which tends to be worse at nights.
She has dropped cups of tea twice in the last month but attributes this to her own clumsiness. She denies any visual, speech, bowel orbladder symptoms. Occasionally she gets some neck discomfort on turning her head but denies any recent or past history of neck trauma.Past medical history includes a left mastectomy 10 years ago for breast cancer. Her sister died of a brain tumour.
On examination, her cranial nerves are intact. No increase in tone is detectable in all limbs. She has mild weakness when ﬂexing thesupinated forearm against resistance, diminished biceps and brachioradialis reﬂexes and increased triceps reﬂexes bilaterally. The rest of hermuscle power and reﬂexes are normal. Plantar responses are ﬂexor bilaterally. Sensory examination is unremarkable to pinprick and jointposition sense.
What is the most likely diagnosis in this woman?
explanation:
The symptoms in this patient best ﬁt a spondylotic problem affecting the C5/6 level, thus the C6 cervical root.
Symptoms and signs of a C6 root lesion includeParaesthesias in the thumb or lateral distal forearmWeakness of brachioradialis, biceps, or triceps andDiminished biceps and brachioradialis reﬂexes in conjunction with an increased triceps reﬂex.
Patients do not always present with all of these features but the key ﬁnding here is the inverted upper limb reﬂexes (brisk triceps anddiminished biceps and brachioradialis).
The presence of sensory symptoms make amyotrophic lateral sclerosis unlikely.
Ulnar nerve entrapment does not cause reﬂex changes.

A 17-year-old girl presented with a two day history of severe back pain.
A plain x ray ﬁlm of her spine is normal. Two days later, she complained of tingling in her ﬁngers and toes. The next day she became generallyweak. She presented in the emergency department.
On examination, she has bilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness, tetraparesis with weakness in all limbs (4/5), areﬂexia, ﬂexor plantarsand normal sensation.

Protein1.4 g/L(<0.4)

Cells 0 (<5 ml)

explanation:
The clinical history is typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Back pain is very common and often severe enough to require opiate treatment.
Acute onset of weakness with areﬂexia and high CSF protein with normal cell count are typical features of the condition.

He was a previously ﬁt young man and was not taking any regular medication. He smoked 10 cigarettes per day and drank approximately 20units of alcohol per week.
On examination, cranial nerves and upper limb examination were entirely normal. Examination of the lower limb revealed good femoralpulses and other distal pulses. Tone appeared normal in both legs. There was reduced power of hip ﬂexion and knee extension on the left,however hip extension and hip adduction and abduction were entirely normal. Power was normal in the right leg. A 28-year-old man was admitted to the Emergency department after attending his weekly judo club meeting.
He had felt well and had been participating actively. Within a few minutes of his ﬁnal ﬁght, he developed pain in his neck, vertigo, blurredvision and diplopia. He had diﬃculty in balancing himself with a tendency to fall to the right and incoordination of right upper and lowerlimbs.
There was accompanying facial asymmetry, decreased hearing from right side, diﬃculty in swallowing, and associated weakness of right sideof body.
There was no past medical history of note and he was a non-smoker.
On examination, a right sided Horner's syndrome was noted. There was nystagmus (fast phase to the right), sensorineural hearing loss in theright ear and paresis of soft palate on right side. There was reduced tone and power in upper and lower limbs on the right. Deep tendonreﬂexes were brisk on the right side and plantar response was extensor.
Sensory examination revealed a crossed hemianaesthesia with involvement of the face on the right side.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vertebral artery dissection is well-recognised cause of stroke in patients under 45 years and is associated with a 10% mortality ratein the acute phase.
Death may occur due to intracranial dissection, brainstem infarction or subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Common causes include:Structural defects of the arterial wallConnective tissue diseaseTrauma (for example, road traﬃc accident, sporting injury), andChiropractic manipulation of the neck.

A 45-year-old publican is admitted to hospital having sustained comminuted fractures of the left femur and tibia. There are no otherapparent injuries. Later that day, following surgical ﬁxation, he becomes aggressive and confused.
His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 110 beats per minute, BP 130/80 mmHg and respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute. He is breathing45% oxygen and his SpO is 90%.
What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
The history and clinical features of this case suggest fat embolism syndrome. Fat embolism syndrome is a clinical diagnosissecondary to the presence of fat globules in the lung parenchyma and circulation that are typically released following long bonefractures. It requires high index of suspicion and usually presents 12-72 hours after initial injury.
There is a classic triad of:Respiratory changes - Dyspnoea, tachypnoea and hypoxaemia are early ﬁndings. These may progress to respiratory failure andARDS requiring mechanical ventilation.Neurological features - Cerebral emboli produce neurological signs in up to 86% cases. They often occur after onset ofrespiratory symptoms, with a wide spectrum ranging from mild confusion and drowsiness to seizures. Usually there is an acuteconfusional state with or without focal signs. Most neurological deﬁcits are transient and reversible.Petechial rash - This is the ﬁnal component of the triad to develop and occurs in 60% of cases. Rash is seen in the conjunctiva,mucous membranes, skin folds of upper body particularly neck and axilla, appearing within the ﬁrst 36 hours.
Patients may also develop:pyrexiatachycardiaECG changes (ST segment depression and right heart strain)ﬂuffy retinal exudates

A 36-year-old man is referred to you with increasing problems with concentration. He also complains of irregular jerky movements of hisextremities and ﬁngers.
He consumes approximately 20 units of alcohol a week. His father was diagnosed with dementia at the age of 40.
Apart from generalised choreiform movements, his neurological and systemic examination was normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Huntington's disease is an autosomally inherited condition due to an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat on the short arm ofchromosome 4. It is characterised by progressive dementia and worsening choreiform movements.
Symptoms typically appear between 30 and 50 years of age.
Genetic testing now provides an accurate method of establishing the diagnosis.
Average life span after clinical onset is about 15 years.

Detailed questioning reveals episodes of blank spells over the last six years and brief shock-like contractions of his upper limbs several timesa month, especially at breakfast times. Past medical and family histories are unremarkable. Physical examination is normal.
Which one of the following treatment options would you consider most appropriate in this patient?
explanation:
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is the commonest of the idiopathic generalised epilepsies.
Seizures types include:AbsencesMyoclonic jerks andTonic-clonic seizures which tend to occur within an hour of waking.
Precipitating factors include alcohol, menstruation and sleep deprivation.
The condition is genetically linked to the short arm of chromosome 6.
Prognosis is extremely favourable if the condition is treated

A 27-year-old man accompanied by his girlfriend was seen by his GP .
Over several months he had begun to hear voices. These voices could be heard at any time. Sometimes the voices would demand him to dothings; sometimes they would hum or laugh. Over the months he had developed the notion that his girlfriend was plotting to leave him andto go and live with his brother. In addition he believed that he had a deadly illness and was unlikely to live for more than a year.
The arguments that followed these 'ideas' had caused a huge rift between him and his girlfriend, as she had been unable to convince himthat they were not true. He had lost over a stone in weight, had become increasingly nervous and was neglecting his appearance.
He had no known medical problems and was not taking any regular medication. He was a smoker of 20 cigarettes per day and drank 15 unitsof alcohol per week. He worked as an accountant, but had recently taken time off sick. He had a sister with depression and epilepsy, butthere were no other known family illnesses.
On examination he appeared withdrawn and unkempt. He continued to ﬁdget with his clothes and continually commented he could smellﬁsh. He was able to talk ﬂuently about his childhood and university years which appeared to be happy times. The death of his mother threeyears ago had been 'diﬃcult'. He scored 30/30 on mini-mental state examination.
Cranial nerve and peripheral nervous system examination did not reveal any abnormalities.
An MRI scan of his brain was normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: This patient presents with a history of hallucinatory voices commanding him to do things, or non-verbal forms such as humming orlaughing.

A 23-year-old ﬁnal year medical student is referred to the outpatient clinic with a two month history of gradual onset left-sided headacheoccurring at least once a week.
The headache which is accompanied by nausea and photophobia prevents her from studying for her examinations.
Which of the following is correct about this person's headache?
options: A family history of similar headaches is common
It responds well to beta agonists
Unilateral tearing and conjunctival injection is a common accompaniment
It is associated with a high ESR
Oxygen inhalation is an appropriate method of treatment
explanation:
In most cases where a family history is present the headache is a migraine. It will respond to beta blockers.
Tearing and conjunctival injection are features of cluster headache for which acute relief may be achieved by inhaling 100% oxygenfor 10-15 minutes.
Temporal arteritis which is associated with a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate is unusual before the age of 60 years.

A 28-year-old shop worker is referred with a three month history of recurrent episodes of disorientation and confusion.
Her boyfriend has found her wandering around the house on several occasions, apparently with no idea of where she is or how she got there.Her mood has been very low, with frequent emotional outbursts, and she has considered leaving her job because of problems with workingthe computer and managing customers' queries. Her boyfriend feels her condition is signiﬁcantly worsening.
Physical examination is normal, apart from recurrent, asymetrical, jerks in all four limbs.
Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in reaching a diagnosis?
explanation:
This kind of rapid cognitive decline in a young person with myoclonus is strongly suggestive of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).
A deﬁnitive diagnosis of any form of CJD requires pathological examination of brain tissue, which is usually only done post-mortem.During life, investigations are undertaken for two reasons: to exclude other possible diagnoses, and to support the diagnosis of CJD.Supportive investigations are EEG, CSF examination and MRI.
The EEG in sporadic CJD may show signiﬁcant abnormalities involving deep brain areas such as the thalami. The normal rhythms aregradually lost. Initially the changes are diffuse, and non-speciﬁc, developing into generalised bi- or triphasic periodic sharp wavecomplexes with a frequency of 1-2 per second. High voltage sharp waves may be synchronous with myoclonic jerks. In anappropriate clinical context, this EEG pattern is strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of CJD.
Neither CSF examination nor MRI are options here, but both can also give supportive information.The CSF typically contains no inﬂammatory cells, but the total protein content may be raised. Analysis for brain speciﬁc proteins,particularly 14-3-3, is supportive in the right clinical context.
In a proportion of cases, abnormalities of signal in the anterior basal ganglia (caudate/putamen, and sometimes the cortex) can beseen on MRI, which can also support the diagnosis.
Chest x ray and liver function tests may help to exclude other diagnoses, but do not give supportive information for CJD.

A 50-year-old man who is known to be a long time heavy drinker is admitted with three generalised convulsive seizures in the space of twohours. He denies any alcohol consumption in the last 48 hours.
There is no other past medical history of note. A CT scan of the brain was unremarkable.
If the patient seizes again, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his condition?
options: Intravenous phenytoin followed by long term oral phenytoin
Intravenous lorazepam followed by long term oral valproate
No antiepileptic drug therapy is indicated
explanation:
The patient is experiencing alcohol withdrawal seizures which typically occur seven to 48 hours after cessation of drinking.
If no underlying structural lesion is detected and the patient does not have an epileptic disorder, no long term antiepileptic drugtherapy is indicated.
However, intravenous administration of lorazepam has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrent seizures.
The absolute risk reduction for recurrence within six hours is 21%.

A 44-year-old man presented to the cardiologists in heart failure. His ECG showed atrial ﬁbrillation at rate of 130 bpm.
He was treated with diuretics and cardioverted with amiodarone. During his admission the nurses noticed that he was walking into objects onthe ward.
On examination there was severe impairment of visual acuity. On direct questioning he denied any visual loss and insisted he was able to seethings around him. CT head showed bilateral occipital infarcts.
What is his diagnosis?
explanation:
Visual anosognosia, or the denial of loss of vision, associated with confabulation in the setting of obvious visual loss and corticalblindness is known as Anton's syndrome.
Claude's syndrome results in ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral cerebellar ataxia and tremor.
Foville's syndrome causes ipsilateral gaze and facial weakness and contralateral hemiparesis of upper and lower limbs.
Parinaud's syndrome causes paralysis of upward gaze and accommodation.
Weber's syndrome results in ipsilateral oculomotor palsy (CN 3 and 4) with contralateral hemiplegia.

A 40-year-old woman is referred to you complaining of a 12 month history of dizziness and unsteadiness, and decreased hearing and tinnitusin her left ear. The dizziness is intermittent in nature and usually lasts for up to two minutes and is vertiginous in nature. Over the last twoweeks, she has also noticed mild diﬃculty closing her left eyelid and her friends have commented that her face is slightly asymmetrical.
On examination, she looks relatively anxious. Cranial nerve examination reveals a reduced left corneal reﬂex, mild diﬃculty in closing theeyelid of her left eye and a slight droop over the left side of her face when she is asked to smile. Hallpike's manoeuvre is negative. Weber'stest reveals lateralisation of the sound to the right ear. Rinne's test reveals air conduction better than bone conduction in both ears. The restof the neurological examination is unremarkable.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The combination of sensorineural deafness, facial nerve palsy and cranial nerve V involvement suggests a cerebellopontine angletumour, for example, acoustic neuroma.
Craniopharyngiomas are more common in children than in adults. Patients usually present with signs of local compression,especially of the visual system, or hypothalamic dysfunction, for example diabetes insipidus or growth failure.
Glomus jugulare tumours tend to present with pulsatile tinnitus and conductive deafness. Cranial nerves IX, X and XI which runthrough the jugular foramen are also commonly affected to varying degrees. Cranial nerves VII and XII may be affected if the tumourenlarges suﬃciently.
Parasagittal meningiomas may produce seizures or be entirely asymptomatic, often growing to enormous size before they arediscovered. Lesions that reach suﬃcient size may cause spastic paraparesis and incontinence.
Prolactinomas commonly present with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea in women and impotence in men. They are also associatedwith visual ﬁeld defects.

A 24-year-old woman presents with an eight week history of headaches, which have deteriorated markedly over the last two days and haveresulted in her admission.
These headaches are distressing to her; they have been problematical in the morning but she has found some relief from paracetamol.However, they are now constant and intolerable. The only other information is that she has gained 6 kg in weight the last six months.
On examination she is noted to be obese with a BMI of 32 kg/m and a blood pressure of 122/76 mmHg. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral
swelling of both optic discs with loss of venous pulsation but otherwise neurological examination is normal. Investigations reveal normal MRIappearances of the brain and a lumbar puncture reveals an opening pressure of 30 cm HO but CSF analysis is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a typical history of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (previously known as benign intracranial hypertension): an obesefemale patient with headaches and papilloedema, normal brain imaging, cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) analysis and high pressure.
The other possible differential diagnosis would be cerebral/sagittal vein thrombosis, but one might expect to pick up evidence forthis on the MRI.

Lower limb examination revealed some mild weakness of hip ﬂexion and extension with marked weakness of dorsiﬂexion and plantarﬂexion.Both knee and ankle jerks were absent and both plantar responses were mute. There was absent sensation to all modalities affecting bothfeet extending to the knees.

A 62-year-old man presented with diﬃcult walking.
He had a past history of diabetes mellitus and cervical spondylosis, which had required surgical decompression eight years previously. Hedrank 40 units of alcohol weekly.
On examination there was fasciculation, wasting and weakness in the left deltoid and biceps, with weakness in the shoulder girdle musclesbilaterally. There was fasciculation in the glutei and quadriceps bilaterally, weakness of hip ﬂexion and foot dorsiﬂexion, brisk reﬂexes inupper and lower limbs, and extensor plantar responses. There was no sensory impairment.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
There are signs of lower (wasting, fasciculations) and upper (brisk reﬂexes, extensor plantar response) motor neurone involvement inthe presence of normal sensation.
Motor neurone disease is the commonest cause of such presentation.
Alcoholic myopathy and diabetic amyotrophy do not share upper motor neurone signs.
Syringomyelia presents with sensory symptoms and signs (spinothalamic).
You expect sensory involvement with cervical cord compression.

A 22-year-old obese woman presented with an eight week history of headaches, pulsatile tinnitus and transient visual loss on standinglasting a few seconds. She had otherwise been well with no history of note.
She took the oral contraceptive pill and had been taking this for the last six months and used salbutamol inhalers on an occasional basis forher asthma which she had from childhood. She also took vitamin A supplements which she bought over the counter for her general health.
On examination, the only abnormality of note was bilateral papilloedema.
MRI brain and MR venogram are normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 38, normal protein, glucose, and cells.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Intracranial hypertension secondary to vitamin A
Sagittal sinus thrombosis secondary to OCP
explanation:
The ﬁndings will be consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (papilloedema, normal cerebrospinal ﬂuid analysis, normalbrain imaging).
Vitamin A is a well known cause of this condition (as well as tetracycline and the oral contraceptive).
